arxiv-2512-00073:
Detecting vehicles at night is hard, and rain makes camera images even noisier. Aswinkumar Varathakumaran and Nirmala Paramanandham present ProvRain in a 2025 study, a system built to clean rainy images and spot vehicles. Their approach looks beyond headlamps, using other features to catch oncoming vehicles earlier.

ProvRain pairs a MobileNet-UNet model for denoising with Faster R-CNN for detection. The cleaning step helps the detector work when rain streaks and low light hide parts of a vehicle. Better night detection supports safer roads, since drivers and driver-assistance systems both need early warning of traffic ahead. The authors frame the system as a step toward dependable perception in bad weather.
arxiv-2512-00373:
Earth and its sibling planets formed from the same disk, yet their bulk compositions differ markedly from simple condensation predictions. Paolo Sossi and co-authors review physicochemical controls on planet compositions in 2025. Metallic cores fix each planet's oxygen fugacity, a measure of its internal oxidation state.

Those values sit far above the oxidation level of the original nebular gas. The review explains which physical and chemical processes drove the planets away from their starting material. Understanding that divergence helps scientists read exoplanet compositions and reconstruct how rocky planets, including Earth, acquired their ingredients. Oxygen fugacity records how oxidized a planet's interior is, a basic chemical fingerprint. For a reader who likes deep time, the tale is a good one. Worlds born from one cloud of dust took on such unlike forms, and the clues lie in their cores.
arxiv-2512-00473:
Text-to-image models follow prompts well, yet their people often look fake, with overly smooth skin and oily sheens. Junyan Ye and co-authors present RealGen in 2025, a method for photorealistic image generation guided by detector-based rewards. Advanced models still show distinct AI artifacts even on simple tasks.

RealGen uses detectors to spot those artifacts and turns their judgments into reward signals for training. Rewarding realism directly attacks the plastic look that prompt engineering cannot fix. More believable generated faces matter for media, advertising, and any setting where synthetic images stand in for photographs. Detector-guided rewards give the generator feedback that pure text matching cannot. Photorealism is the specific gap the authors target, not image quality in general.
arxiv-2512-00573:
Higher spin fields extend the usual cast of particles and forces, and supersymmetry doubles the stage again. A 2025 study develops higher spin theory with extended supersymmetry using harmonic superspace methods. Harmonic superspace was introduced in 1984 for describing supersymmetric field theories geometrically.

The harmonic approach gives an off-shell description of supersymmetric theories, covering Yang-Mills theory, supergravity, and matter with spins up to two. Extending it to higher spins tests whether those exotic fields can interact consistently. The work sits at the foundations of supersymmetry and quantum field theory. Off-shell descriptions keep all symmetries visible, which higher spin theories badly need. The maximal spins of the classic theories are one, two, and one half. The work is deep theory, and its worth is in the base it lays. If such fields can play well with the known ones, new doors in physics may open.
arxiv-2512-00773:
Toshiki Katsube and five coauthors present DEJIMA, a large Japanese dataset for vision and language, in a 2025 paper. Models that caption images or answer questions about them need lots of good training data. For Japanese, such large, high-quality resources have been scarce.

The team built a pipeline that collects web images at scale, then filters and deduplicates them with care. It pulls evidence from object detection and uses large language models to refine the text, under rules that keep text tied to the image. DEJIMA gives Japanese vision-language research a firmer base to train and test on.
arxiv-2512-00973:
John Douglas Moore generalizes a classic geometry theorem in a 2025 math paper. Hilbert's theorem says the hyperbolic plane, a surface of constant negative curvature, cannot be placed inside ordinary three-dimensional space without distortion. Moore works with submanifolds of constant negative curvature in higher dimensions.

He uses the generalized Gauss-Bonnet formula for Riemannian polyhedra, discovered by Allendoerfer, Weil, and Chern. With it, he shows hyperbolic space of dimension n has no isometric immersion into Euclidean space of dimension twice n minus one. Such no-go results draw a firm line between what curved spaces can and cannot do inside flat space. The result shows how much room curved spaces need when they sit in flat ones.
arxiv-2512-01173:
Shiho Oi and Kaito Sato study special maps between function spaces in a 2025 math paper. The Wiener algebra collects functions whose Fourier series converge absolutely, a well-behaved class used in analysis. Its positive cone holds the functions in it that take nonnegative values, in the sense used there.

The authors study surjective maps between such cones that preserve the spectrum of the sum of any two elements. They show these maps extend to isometric real-linear isomorphisms of the whole algebra. In plain terms, preserving a small amount of spectral data forces the map to be rigid and fully structured.
arxiv-2512-01573:
Meiqing Zhong, Cui Meng, and Yinong Liu test how combined pulses harm a common transistor. A vertical NPN bipolar transistor faced X-ray bursts and electromagnetic pulses at once. Each stress alone is known. Together they may do more harm than the sum.

Lab tests under pulsed X-rays measured the damage. Computer-aided design simulations traced the physics inside. A positive pulse case showed clear combined effects. Knowing how the two stresses add helps harden circuits for space, defense, and nuclear settings where both can strike. Pulse shape and timing both matter, so the tests vary each in turn to see which one drives the transistor toward failure first.
arxiv-2512-01773:
Chenghao Gu and co-authors generate robot training data from open-world images. Generalist robot policies need vast training data. Collecting data on real robots is slow and tied to one setting. Open images hold huge scene variety that matches manipulation tasks well.

Their IGen frame turns such images into robot learning data at scale. Scenes from the wild supply objects, layouts, and contexts. Generated data can pretrain policies before costly robot time. That path could widen robot skills to homes and shops that no lab can rebuild. Image-derived data also spans rare scenes, like disaster zones, where robot trials cannot be staged but photos exist in bulk.
arxiv-2512-01873:
Fractional Chern insulators are exotic quantum materials that host unusual states of matter, but predicting which settings will support them is hard. A 2025 paper by Oriol Mayné i Comas and co-authors builds a data-driven way to judge their stability from the geometry of a material's energy bands.

Using large-scale exact calculations, the team scores stability across a wide range of settings, producing a smooth measure rather than a yes-or-no label. Machine learning then refines simpler rule-of-thumb predictors against that measure, while staying readable enough for physicists to interpret. The result is a clearer map of where these fragile quantum states can survive.
arxiv-2512-01973:
Checking whether a multi-threaded recursive program can reach a bad state is, in general, impossible to decide. C. Aiswarya and four co-authors study this reachability problem for multi-pushdown automata in 2025, a model equivalent to interleaved Dyck reachability, widely used in program analysis.

Because the full problem is undecidable, researchers build decidable under-approximations that still catch real errors. The authors bring in bounded treewidth and multiple context-free grammars, two structural tools for taming such systems, along with downward closures. Their results help draw the line between program properties that verification tools can settle and those they provably cannot.
arxiv-2512-02073:
Graph contrastive learning teaches a model what makes a graph itself by comparing altered views of it that should still match. Qirui Ji and seven co-authors present HTG-GCL in 2025, a method that reads a graph's topology at several levels of detail, from fine to coarse.

Existing methods that alter graph structure often miss the topological patterns a task actually needs, and different tasks need different levels of detail. The authors extract hierarchical topological granularity from cellular complexes, richer structures built on top of graphs, and feed it into the contrast. Respecting topology at the right scale should yield graph representations that transfer better across chemistry, biology, and network tasks.
arxiv-2512-02273:
Text-to-video models have learned to generate smooth, plausible motion, and that talent may double as a repair kit for damaged images. Peng Kang, Xijun Wang, and Yu Yuan repurpose the video model CogVideo in 2025 for progressive image restoration, fine-tuning it to produce restoration trajectories instead of natural motion.

The damaged image is treated as the first frame of a short film whose final frame is the restored picture. Generating the in-between steps gradually may recover detail more gracefully than a single leap. The study opens a new use for video generation's temporal strength, suggesting that restoration is really motion through quality space.
arxiv-2512-02473:
Yuta Oshima and colleagues at the University of Tokyo study video models that predict what a scene will look like next. Given past views and a move, such as turning left, a world model paints the next frames. Keeping those frames steady over space and time has stayed hard for years.

Long scenes need long input, and long input costs too much computing power to use directly. The team's WorldPack method squeezes memory into a compact form the model can carry along. That compressed memory helps the video stay consistent as the view moves through space. Steadier video helps robots and games that must act on what they see.
arxiv-2512-02773:
S. O. Kara builds a precision ready framework for new forces that talk only to leptons. In this extension, leptons carry family dependent charges under a new symmetry, while quarks stay neutral. Keeping the theory consistent requires a minimal set of vectorlike leptons.

Kara connects those high energy interactions to their low energy fingerprints in standard effective theories. The translation lets precision data, from meson decays to collider runs, test the idea fairly. Model independent bridges like this help experiments squeeze meaning from null results and guide where to look next. Clean links from high scale law to low scale data let null finds bite, which is how most new laws fall in the end.
arxiv-2512-02873:
Luca Di Stefano extends automata that read endless streams over huge alphabets. Extensions of omega automata handle infinite inputs, using symbolic guards to keep transitions finite. Registers can carry past values forward, but their formal semantics grow intricate and tractability suffers.

Symbolic transitions alone, though, cannot act well on stored information. Di Stefano's obligations offer another way to track duties across a run. Cleaner machinery for infinite streams supports verification of reactive systems, like controllers and protocols that must run forever without a final state. Clean rules for streams that run on and on are the base on which proofs for live rigs will rest in years to come.
arxiv-2512-03073:
Open AI models have grown fast since 2019. Shayne Longpre and seven co-authors trace that growth in this 2025 study. They focus on Hugging Face, the main global site where open models are shared.

The authors share a full record of weekly model downloads from mid 2020 to late summer 2025, plus model details. With that record they test how much power sits with a few makers. They also track how the open model world has changed over time. The data help readers judge who shapes open AI and who takes part. Its download record also lets readers see which firms and labs release models most often, and how that lead shifts over time.
arxiv-2512-03173:
What an object is for depends on culture. Joan Nwatu, Longju Bai, Oana Ignat, and Rada Mihalcea study that fact in this 2025 work. Image and language data sets tend to favor rich, Western settings, which skews what AI models learn.

That skew can hurt people in lower-income and non-Western places. The authors build a culture affordance atlas that maps objects to their uses across cultures. The atlas aims to reconcile diverse uses of the same object. Fairer data could help vision and language tools serve all users better. An atlas format lets model builders audit training data for gaps across regions and incomes.
arxiv-2512-03273:
A simple game of balance leads to deep math questions. Imre Bárány and Jeck Lim study balancing games on unbounded sets in this 2025 work. They define a set as closed under a step rule tied to a finite set of moves.

Given a point in the set and a move, at least one of adding or subtracting the move stays in the set. The authors explore what structures satisfy that rule. Such games connect geometry, number theory, and combinatorics. Their results may inform tiling and discrepancy problems. Closed sets under such rules form rich structures from a very simple demand.
arxiv-2512-03373:
AI-written ads may persuade as well as human ones, or better. Elyas Meguellati and co-authors test that claim in this 2025 work. As language models grow better at persuasive text, firms need to know how their ads perform.

The study looks at ads through two lenses. One is personality-based targeting, the other is psychological persuasion principles. Comparing the two shows where model ads match or beat personalization. The results matter for marketing practice and for rules on AI use in advertising. Personality and persuasion tests together show whether gains come from targeting or from craft.
arxiv-2512-03473:
Supersymmetric theories break in subtle ways worth mapping. Digvijay Roy Varier, Zijian Gu, Bea Noether, and Hitoshi Murayama study one such theory in this 2025 work. They examine symplectic QCD with several flavors, perturbed by anomaly mediated supersymmetry breaking.

The team studies minima where chiral symmetry breaks, plus other potential minima. Knowing which minimum wins decides the theory's low-energy behavior. Careful study avoids false conclusions from shallow minima. The results add to the map of how supersymmetric gauge theories behave when softly broken. Other minima can trap naive analyses, so mapping them all is essential groundwork.
arxiv-2601-06873: Research by Mustafa Abdool and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with applying Embedding-Based retrieval to airbnb search. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The goal of Airbnb search is to match guests with the ideal accommodation that fits their travel needs. This is a challenging problem, as popular search locations can have around a hundred thousand available homes. And guests themselves have a wide variety of preferences. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-06973:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Davide Baldelli and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers LLMs can’t play hangman. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. As LLMs move from text completion toward autonomous agents, they remain constrained by the standard chat interface, which lacks private working memory.

This raises a fundamental question: can agents reliably perform interactive tasks that depend on hidden state. We define Private State Interactive Tasks (PSITs), which require agents to generate and maintain hidden information while producing consistent public responses. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07373:
Muhammad Raza and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with enumeration of generalized cospectral mates of graphs. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The work investigates the enumeration of generalized cospectral mates of simple graphs. Where the generalized spectrum consists of the spectra of a graph and its complement.

Moving beyond the classical problem of identifying graphs determined by their generalized spectrum. We address the more quantitative question of how many non-isomorphic graphs can share the same generalized spectrum. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07473:
Michael J. Clark introduces AntiPaSTO, a method for steering language models toward honesty, in a 2026 preprint. As models grow more capable, people cannot easily check what they say. Steering methods therefore need to work from inside the model, without constant human labels. They also need to hold up on new kinds of inputs.

Existing methods, Clark notes, meet only some of those demands. AntiPaSTO is self-supervised and separates internal representations along an antiparallel axis. Pushing one way or the other along that axis shifts behavior in opposite directions. Coherence constraints keep the model from collapsing into nonsense. The paper speaks to the wider effort to keep advanced models truthful and controllable.
arxiv-2601-07773:
Lingchen Sun and coauthors train diffusion transformers with signals that sit inside the model. Recent work guides diffusion models with outside semantic features, such as those from DINO. That guidance can greatly speed training. It also needs pretrained outside networks, which adds links to other tools and cuts freedom. Their 2026 preprint seeks the same gain from features found inside instead.

The title speaks of freeing the rich meaning that sits inside diffusion transformers. If inner layers already encode useful semantics, training can lean on them directly. With no outside teacher, the pipeline gets simpler and needs less compute tied to a second model. Faster diffusion training matters because these models are costly to build. The paper targets generative modeling scholars. It asks whether the guide a model needs has been inside it all along. The gain, if it holds, is a lean build with fewer parts to keep in step.
arxiv-2601-07973:
Myra Cheng and colleagues build a framework for organizing social norms so AI norm violations can be detected. Generative AI should be useful and safe across cultures. Understanding how models follow sociocultural norms is a key step. Existing NLP work, they note, lacks nuance and coverage in evaluating norm adherence. Their 2026 preprint, Cultural Compass, addresses that gap for human-AI conversations.

Norms vary by culture and situation, so a flat rule list fails. A compass framework organizes norms so violations can be spotted in context. Detection is a prerequisite for training or steering models to behave appropriately. The work matters for products deployed across many countries at once. The paper serves NLP scholars and AI safety teams. It supplies structure for a topic often handled with ad hoc lists.
arxiv-2601-08073: Bandar Al-Dhalaan and Shalev Ben-David study turning Monte Carlo methods into Las Vegas methods for composed functions. Their 2026 arXiv paper works with Boolean functions and query complexity measures. For a measure M and function f, they define a composition limit as the number of compositions grows without bound. Monte Carlo algorithms may err, while Las Vegas algorithms always give correct answers with random run time. The paper asks when recursive composition lets one style be converted into the other. It serves readers in theoretical computer science.
arxiv-2601-08573: Andrea Braides wrote a 2026 arXiv paper that sums up new results on a tool for hard math problems. The tool is singular perturbations of non-convex functionals. When a problem has many best answers, a small added term can pick out one of them. The classic case is the gradient theory of phase transitions by Modica. That theory built on Gamma-convergence work by Modica and Mortola. It backed the minimal-interface rule for phase lines. The paper sums up fresh work on the non-local form of the tool.
arxiv-2601-08673:
Didier Sornette, Sandro Claudio Lera, and Ke Wu argue that AI alignment failure is structural, not accidental. Their 2026 arXiv paper responds to reports of language models showing deception, threats, or blackmail. Such reports are often read as proof of alignment failure or emergent malign agency.

The authors argue that this reading rests on a conceptual error. Models learn human interaction structures, including manipulation patterns present in training data. Advanced AI then acts as an endogenous evolutionary shock to the systems it joins. The paper reframes safety debates: if failure is structural, fixes must target training structures and deployment incentives, not just individual model misbehavior.
arxiv-2601-08873:
Hema Hariharan Samson builds a tool to spot fake or cut images across many sources. Old check tools work on one class of flaw. A tool trained on phone shots may fail on AI art or on scans. Real check work must cross those lines each day. Samson aims for one tool that holds up in all of them.

The tool is called ForensicFormer. It reads an image at three scales at once. Fine scale checks catch pixel flaws. Mid scale checks read edge breaks. Large scale checks ask if the scene makes sense. Past tools that use one scale fell below a set mark on new sets. This tool holds a high mark on those sets, the author says. A reader in image checks gets a broad, layered plan.
arxiv-2601-09473:
Oliver Bolton and five co-authors, including Sara Hooker, automate a choice that language model builders now face often. Their 2026 arXiv paper, SimMerge, learns to select merge operators from similarity signals. Model merging blends several trained models into one that keeps their combined skills.

Scaling merging is hard because quality depends on the operator, the subset of models, and the merge order. Testing each option by merging and evaluating is costly. SimMerge instead reads similarity signals between models and predicts a good recipe. A cheap selector would make merging a routine step in building capable models.
arxiv-2601-09873:
Saymon Souza, Amanda Santana, and Eduardo Figueiredo test whether language models can smell bad code. Their 2026 arXiv paper assesses large language models for code smell detection, moving beyond strict rule-based checkers. Code smells are warning signs of quality problems that raise maintenance costs.

Language models have shown skill across many software engineering tasks. Their use for smell detection is still little explored. The authors measure how effective the models are in practice. A capable detector tool could warn developers very early on, before smelly code hardens into expensive, unreliable systems.
arxiv-2601-09973:
Samuel Everett links two hard fields: how hard a task is, and how a flow acts. His tasks ask if a point can reach a set in finite time. The flow is one way and sits on a line. Each task comes from its own flow.

He shows a tight link. If tasks from two flows can map to each other in a natural way, the flows must act alike. The word alike is made sharp in the proof. The paper is part two of a pair. It gives a tool to sort flows by the tasks they spawn.
arxiv-2601-10373:
Yichong Xia, Yimin Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, and Bin Chen squeeze images to a trickle of bits. New diffusion tools can rebuild a rich image from few bits. The rebuilt shot looks true to the eye. But past tools are slow to sample. Their bit splits are also oft poor.

The team made DiffCR, a squeeze frame built for speed. It refines a diffusion prior in a firm way. That cuts the slow sample steps. It also splits bits with more care across the image. The aim is a small file that rebuilds fast and looks true.
arxiv-2601-10673:
Aditya Agrawal and a team at Google tackle a bottleneck in training and serving large language models. Model data must be split across many accelerator chips. The collective steps that sync those chips are often capped by network bandwidth. Faster compression of the data in flight would ease that cap.

The team presents a single-stage Huffman encoder built for machine learning compression. Huffman coding squeezes data by giving short codes to common values. A one-stage design aims to keep the squeeze fast enough for live training traffic. If it holds up, big model runs could spend less time waiting on the network.
arxiv-2601-10773:
Niko Usai, Dario Montagnini, Kristian Ilianov Iliev, and Raffaele Camanzo present LogicLens, a tool for grasping large software systems. Big systems sprawl across many repositories and microservices. To reason about them, developers need more than code structure. They need the domain logic and runtime behavior, which sit implicit and scattered across the codebase.

LogicLens builds a semantic code graph to explore such systems. A graph can join calls, data, and intent in one view. That helps new team members and auditors find how a feature truly works. The work speaks to engineers who inherit sprawling systems and must change them without breaking hidden links.
arxiv-2601-11073:
Rongkun Cui, Nana Zhang, Kun Zhu, and Qi Zhang build a hypergraph learning system to catch web finance fraud. Online finance is a core part of the web economy. Its openness invites fraud that harms vulnerable users and weakens trust in digital finance. The authors draw their design from the hippocampus, the brain region that binds memories together.

Their multi-view hypergraph model links accounts, devices, and transactions in shared hyperedges. Views from several angles help expose fraud rings that single links hide. The brain-inspired framing stresses memory: fraud patterns repeat, and a system that recalls them can flag new variants. The work serves platforms that must police harm without freezing honest users out.
arxiv-2601-11573:
Muhammad Muneeb and David Ascher fine-tune language models on bioinformatics text. Their 2026 preprint gives a reproducible pipeline for the work. General LLMs often lack specialized knowledge for this field. Bioinformatics tasks need tool names, data forms, and jargon.

Two use cases show the pipeline in action. PRSGPT focuses on polygenic risk score tools and their use. BioStarsGPT trains on community forum discussions instead. Forum text holds practical know-how from working analysts. The pipeline can be rerun by other teams on new data. That reproducibility is a stated design goal of the work. Specialist models may then serve niche science better.
arxiv-2601-11773:
Elliot Benjamin and Mohamed Mahmoud Chems-Eddin work on a deep question in number theory. They study real quadratic fields, which add a square root to the rationals. For each field, a tower of class fields can be built step by step. They ask how long that tower runs.

They pick fields whose class group is a small group of order four. They also pick fields whose discriminant is not a sum of two squares. The work is a follow-up, checking past guesses on tower length. Such towers test how class groups grow in pure maths.
arxiv-2601-12273:
Chihiro Yoshida, Yuta Ishimoto, Olivier Nourry, and their co-authors use mutation analysis to guide LLM repair of quantum programs. Repair tools for quantum code exist, but they often fail or make patches that are hard to read. Mutation analysis seeds small faults to test a repair.

Those seeded faults can steer a language model to the true flaw. A guided search may lift repair rates and yield clearer patches. Quantum code is hard to debug by hand, so such help is prized. The work tests the pairing on quantum programs.
arxiv-2601-12773:
Lea S. Schimak and eleven co authors test red clump star models with a rare binary system. Binaries where both stars pulsate are rare but extremely valuable. Their system pairs a core helium burning red clump star with a red giant branch star. The binary is cataloged as KIC 10841730, and it pulsates in ways seismology can read.

Theirs is the first study of an asteroseismic binary of this exact makeup. Asteroseismology uses star vibrations to probe interiors that light cannot reach. Two pulsating stars in one system give cross checks no single star can. Red clump stars serve as standard candles for galactic distances. Testing their models sharpens the distance ladder of astronomy.
arxiv-2601-13173:
Leonardo Grimaldi, Elisa Maggio, Lorenzo Pompili, and Alessandra Buonanno test Einstein's theory with a loud black hole crash. The signal, named GW250114, is the clearest wave of its kind yet caught. Its last stage, where the merged hole rings down, is a sharp probe of strong gravity.

The team asks how well that stage fits Einstein's rules for holes that spin and wobble. They use a wave form model that can bend away from Einstein's form in set ways. It sits in the effective one body frame, a way to map two body motion to one body terms. Tight bounds here would be a strong pass for the theory in its most harsh realm yet.
arxiv-2601-13473:
A. Koley, A. M. Stutz, and co-authors map magnetic fields in the G327.29 star forming cluster two ways. Fields and churn may steer how such clusters make dense cores and stars. To test that role, the field's shape in space must be known with care.

One read uses the velocity gradient technique on molecular line light. A next read uses polarized light from dust in the same sky. The team sets the two maps side by side. Where they match, trust grows. Where they part, the part marks a limit of one tool. ALMA data drives both reads. Such a head to head test firms up field maps for all cluster work.
arxiv-2601-14173:
Paris Karakasis and Nicholas Sidiropoulos study smoothness penalties for low-rank tensor models in 2026. Their models are low-rank tensor-product B-spline models for regression tasks. They investigate Dirichlet energy as a measure of smoothness. They show these models admit a closed-form expression for that energy.

They also reveal scenarios where perfect interpolation is possible with tiny Dirichlet energy. Exponentially small energy can accompany an exact fit in those cases. That renders global Dirichlet energy regularization ineffective as a guard. Local penalties, per the title, offer a way to restore control. The fix is to charge for rough spots where they sit, not for the whole field. That local charge keeps good fits sharp while it curbs the cheat.
arxiv-2601-14473:
Danny Butvinik, Nana Boateng, and Achi Hackmon study financial crime queues in this 2026 paper. Detection systems turn a continuous stream of risk scores into decision thresholds. Scores must be split into priority classes for investigators. The catch is that score distributions are non-stationary: they drift over time, so fixed thresholds go stale.

The team proposes adaptive kernel density estimation for real-time thresholding. KDE is a way to estimate the shape of a score distribution from live data. Their system builds prioritized queues for financial crime investigation. Readers get a method that keeps alert queues stable and sorted even as fraud patterns shift under them.
arxiv-2601-14573:
M. N. Chernodub, V. A. Goy, and A. V. Molochkov simulate the electroweak model in a strong magnetic field in this 2026 paper. They use numerical Monte Carlo simulations on a lattice. Their goal is the mass spectrum of the bosonic sector of the model. The external field has electroweak-scale strength, about 10 to the 20th tesla. The temperature is zero.

Fields that strong exist only in extreme settings, such as the early universe or magnetars. The paper's title asks a pointed question: are there acoustic phonons in a magnetized vacuum? Phonons are sound-like waves in a medium. Readers get lattice results on how the vacuum itself behaves as a material under such a field.
arxiv-2601-14673:
Yogesh Pipada Sunil Kumar and four co-authors bring neural networks into power system optimization in this 2026 paper. The decarbonisation of power systems drives growing reliance on distributed energy resources. Those resources introduce complex, nonlinear interactions. Conventional optimization models struggle to capture them. Machine learning based surrogate modelling has emerged as a promising approach.

The catch comes at integration time. Embedding ReLU deep neural networks directly into optimization often results in nonconvex and computationally intractable formulations. The team develops efficient reformulations of such networks for surrogate modelling. Reformulation rewrites the network so solvers can handle it. The point is use. A net that no solver can read is a dead end for grid work, no matter how well it fits past data. That is the goal of the work. Readers get a bridge between trained neural surrogates and the optimizers that run real grids.
arxiv-2601-14773:
Haizhou Liu, Yiming Wang, Haodong Jin, and Hui Yu summarize videos with AI in this 2026 paper. Video summarization enables efficient browsing of massive multimedia content and extraction of key information from social platforms. Most existing unsupervised summarization methods rely on Generative Adversarial Networks. GANs enhance keyframe selection and generate coherent summaries through adversarial training.

The team's method is semantic-guided unsupervised video summarization. Semantic guidance means the summary follows meaning, not just visual change. Unsupervised means no human-made summaries are needed for training. The use is plain. A long clip can be cut to its key frames, so a viewer saves time. Readers get a summarizer aimed at social video, where meaning matters more than motion: the key moment may be a quiet one.
arxiv-2601-14873:
Youssef El Khatiri works in the algebra of operators, the math behind much of quantum theory. His 2026 arXiv paper studies C*-algebras, a key class of these algebras. He looks at maps that keep the order between elements of the algebra.

El Khatiri gives a full account of such order-preserving maps. He covers maps between the self-adjoint parts of two C*-algebras. He then extends the result to general operator intervals in a wider class of algebras. The account rests on Jordan maps and on closed operators in rings tied to the algebra.
arxiv-2601-15173:
Katarina Krivokuća bounds a covering quantity for convex bodies. Her 2026 arXiv paper deals with the covering minima of a convex body, a gauge from the geometry of numbers. She gives two new upper bounds for that quantity.

Each bound leans on simpler pieces of the body. One uses the covering minima of its projections. The other uses its intersections with flat subspaces. She shows one bound is sharp for direct sums of two bodies. That sharp case extends earlier results on covering radius and on lattice width for such sums.
arxiv-2601-15473:
Fahd Seddik and four co-authors tackle a tooling gap in deep learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Training large models strains GPU memory and compute budgets. Methods from randomized numerical linear algebra, or RandNLA, can help shrink these models. Yet no single, production-grade library has pulled those methods together. That gap, the authors argue, has slowed wider use.

Their answer is Panther, a library that works with PyTorch. Panther gathers known RandNLA methods into one fast framework. The title promises faster and cheaper computation as the payoff. For model builders, the point is plain. Tricks that once took custom code now sit in one shared tool, ready to use.
arxiv-2601-15673:
Qilong Yan and four co-authors improve recommendation with diffusion models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Sequential recommendation predicts what a user will want next. Methods have grown more complex over time. Many now use diffusion-guided generation instead of plain classification. These methods lean on user information as guidance. Real user sequences have missing data, though. Gaps in that guidance hurt the quality of what gets generated.

The title names the focus: enhancing guidance when data are missing. Better guidance should steer generation toward items the user truly wants. Missing history is the norm in real platforms, not the exception. Users skip, pause, and browse off the record. A recommender that copes with holes serves both users and sellers better.
arxiv-2601-15773:
Yuanyuan Qi and six co-authors blend several language models into active learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Active learning picks which data humans should label. Language models now join these pipelines as annotators. Their labels cut annotation costs. Quality is the catch. Labels from models often fall short of real-world needs. One model alone can be biased or brittle.

The title names the fix: a mixture of LLMs in the loop. Several models label together, checking each other's weak spots. Diversity among annotators is a classic route to better labels. The authors aim for annotation that stays cheap without going sloppy. Labeled data feed nearly every applied AI project. Cutting its cost while holding quality is a broad win.
arxiv-2601-16473:
Wei Song and coauthors strip deepfake marks with no query to the guard. Their 2026 preprint, named DeMark, deals with marks hid in fake pics. Marks let teams spot fakes and trace their source. The guard case holds that marks stand firm to clean tricks. Past tests oft need asks to the guard model to find a path.

DeMark needs no such asks to strip the mark. A no ask attack is far more hard to spot or block. If marks fall with ease, mark guards need a rethink. The work tests mark strength in a harsh, real case. It warns teams that marks alone may not hold.
arxiv-2601-17373:
Shuning Zhang and seven co-authors study privacy fears in smart home assistants. These tools now act as social agents in the home. User worry turns on where data goes and who can hear it. The team uses Privacy Boundary Theory, a frame from interpersonal talk. A three-phase early study grounds their work. It first maps how data moves in these homes.

From that base, they probe how risk feels across sharing ranges. A chat kept in one room feels unlike one sent to the cloud. Design that shows those ranges could calm real fears. It could also stop over-sharing by default. The work links social theory to device design.
arxiv-2601-17673:
Weiyu Zhang, Yuan Hu, Yong Li, and Yu Liu present Uni-RS for remote sensing. Unified models both understand and generate images. The authors name a flaw they call the spatial reversal curse. Models can describe object locations in images with care. Yet they fail to use the same spatial relations when they generate. In remote sensing, those relations are core meaning.

A map-like image with wrong left-right layout is useless. Uni-RS aims for spatial faithfulness in both directions. Better spatial truth serves land use, disaster, and defense maps. Generation that respects layout can also augment training data. The work names a clear failure mode. Naming it lets the field measure progress on it.
arxiv-2601-17973:
Yuan Bian, Grace Y. Yi, and Wenqing He extend boosting to data where event times are only partly known. Their 2026 preprint deals with interval-censored data. In such data, an event is known to fall inside a window, but the exact time is unseen. The setup is common in survival analysis and in studies of time to an event, like relapse or failure. Classic boosting was built for full data and often struggles here.

Boosting builds a strong model by joining many weak ones in steps. The authors adapt that idea for both regression and classification with censored inputs. Sound tools for windowed data matter in medicine and reliability work. The paper gives those fields a modern learning option.
arxiv-2601-18173: N. B. Huamaní studies vertex degrees in grid graphs built from permutations that avoid the pattern 213. His 2026 preprint builds the graph column by column, with each column's height set by the permutation entry. Vertical edges join levels inside a column, and horizontal edges join equal levels in neighboring columns. The paper works out how the degrees of the vertices behave in this family.
arxiv-2601-18273:
Lorenzo Verzichelli works on scaling normalizing flows to bigger problems in condensed matter. His 2026 preprint studies the Hubbard model, a basic model of electrons in a lattice. Normalizing flows have recently learned the Boltzmann distribution of that model. That success opens a new route to generative modeling of quantum materials. The open question is how to reach larger lattices and lower temperatures without the training falling apart.

Verzichelli studies the steps needed for that scale-up. Stability and efficiency are his twin focus. Flows that stay sound at low temperature could sample states that other methods reach slowly. The work maps the path from a proof of concept to a working tool.
arxiv-2601-18573:
Frederik Glitzner and David Manlove study match tasks in which some who take part break ranks and some hold firm. The base tasks pair up people by what they like best, in a way no pair would both gain by a swap. In one form of the task such a firm match is sure to exist and can be found fast. In the next form it may not exist at all, though one can tell fast if it does.

Real match tasks must weigh size next to firm-ness: a big match that some would break, or a small one that none would. The team add two kinds of folk to that mix. Some will break a match for a small gain. Some will hold firm at a cost. Their maths maps how those kinds shift the best trade. Match maths serves dorms, jobs, and organ swaps.
arxiv-2601-18873:
A study sets out a new kind of skyrmion that is born of heat, not of cold calm. A skyrmion is a knot in a field that can't be smoothed out. It acts like a lone bit and can be quite firm. In the maths of the bits that fill atom cores, such knots stand for the cores them-selves. They may also live in the field that gives mass to all bits, if set cross terms are at play.

The new kind is tied to heat: its form and firm-ness shift with how hot the field runs. That tie could change where such knots can live and what they do. Heat-born knots may have played a role in the hot young cosmos. The work is a maths study, with no lab test in view. It adds a fresh form to a prized class of field knots.
arxiv-2601-19073:
Jessica Eskew and eight co-authors study how a split in a magnetic island changes the spread of electrons. In magnetized plasmas, islands are closed loops of field that can trap or guide particles. When an island splits, its inner points and borders move, and the paths for sideways diffusion change with them.

The team tracks that effect under controlled splitting of the island shape. Diffusion across the field sets how fast heat and particles leak in fusion and space plasmas. Knowing how island shape steers that leak helps read experiments and may help keep hot plasma penned in longer.
arxiv-2601-19473:
Lucia Varbaro and thirteen co-authors report superconductivity that returns, driven by magnetism, in a nickel based crystal. Infinite layer nickelates are thin structured cousins of the famous cuprate superconductors. Doping this one with europium adds magnetic atoms to the mix.

In such a setting, superconductivity can vanish and then come back, a re-entrance, as conditions shift. The team traces that return and links it to the paramagnetic response of the dopants. Re-entrant cases are stress tests for theories of how magnetism and superconductivity share one material, a puzzle at the heart of the field.
arxiv-2601-19973:
Andrew R. Casey and five colleagues rethink a routine step in analysing starlight. To infer a star's temperature and chemistry, astronomers forward-model its spectrum. That usually requires a synthesis code or an emulator trained on curated examples. Before modelling, the spectrum is normalised: its continuum level is set by a preprocessing step kept separate from the stellar parameters.

That separation biases results and makes them inconsistent across signal-to-noise levels. The authors propose a constrained linear model that folds continuum normalisation into the analysis itself. A joint treatment should give abundances that agree no matter how noisy the data are. Chemical surveys of millions of stars depend on such consistency. The work cleans up a quiet source of systematic error. The bias is small but it does not go away.
arxiv-2601-20173:
Zeyang Huang and four colleagues present MAPLE, a method that squeezes high-dimensional data down to a low-dimensional map for visual analysis. It builds on UMAP, a widely used tool for this task. MAPLE adds self-supervised learning to model the shape of the data manifold more efficiently.

At its core are maximum manifold capacity representations. These pull together points that are locally similar while pushing apart points that differ. The result is a map where tangled structure is easier to see. Better maps help analysts explore data in fields from biology to social science, where clusters and paths guide the next questions.
arxiv-2601-20473:
Weichen Wang and a large team report a quiet galaxy. It sits inside a gas-rich knot of the cosmic web at redshift about three, when the universe was young. Space telescopes have recently found many quenched galaxies at that era, which challenges models of galaxy formation. Since star formation feeds on gas flowing in from outside, the gas around such a galaxy is the key clue.

This galaxy sits where filaments of the web meet and gas is plentiful, yet it has stopped forming stars. Studying its circumgalactic gas may show how quenching can win even where fuel is abundant.
arxiv-2601-20673:
Felix Janda and Xin Wang study deep patterns in the geometry of curves in this 2026 math paper. Their subject is topological recursion relations on the moduli space of curves. That space collects all curves of a given genus with marked points. Recursion relations are formulas that tie complex cases to simpler ones. The paper looks at the basic structures these relations can take.

One focus is the coefficient of the bouquet class on that space. That coefficient gives the answer to a conjecture in the field. The authors map out the structures one by one. Their work is pure geometry, aimed at readers who study how these spaces are built. It adds basic facts that later work on curve spaces can build on.
arxiv-2601-20773:
Rubén Jiménez and Oriol Pujol copy deployed AI models using nothing but questions and answers. Their 2026 paper studies black-box model copying with signed-distance supervision. Deployed systems must evolve as data, architectures, and regulations change. Often the original training data and model internals are gone. Black-box copying offers a practical refactoring path. A replica is learned from input-output queries alone. The legacy model is upgraded without ever being opened.

The authors smooth that copying with signed-distance supervision. A signed distance says how far an input sits from a decision boundary, and on which side. That richer signal guides the replica beyond bare labels. Better copies preserve behavior where it matters most. The method serves teams stuck with models they cannot retrain. It turns a black box into a maintainable asset.
arxiv-2601-20873: P. J. Rijken and Th. A. Rijken give a new way to find the eigenvalues of the Heun equation. Eigenvalues are the special values at which an equation has clean solutions. The Heun equation is a broad form met across physics. Its eigenvalues are hard to pin down. The 2026 paper tests the method on the Breit equation, a two-particle equation from atomic physics.
arxiv-2601-21273:
Tianchen Hu and ten co-authors test how a layered crystal handles very strong light pulses. The crystal belongs to a family with built-in electric order and strong responses to light. Earlier work focused on its simpler response, where light comes out at twice the input frequency.

The team measures stronger effects, where the output reaches much higher multiples of the input frequency. Such high harmonics can serve as tiny light sources and probes of the material itself. The crystal's layered form makes it a good fit for small devices. The results support its use in compact photonics, where strong light effects must fit on a chip.
arxiv-2601-21373:
V.L. Martinez-Consentino, J.E. Amaro, and J. Segovia compute how nuclei answer when neutrinos scatter off pairs of particles inside them. Two particles can be knocked out together by exchange currents between nucleons. That two-body response is a key input for reading neutrino experiments.

The authors study how the response scales across many nuclei, from helium up to uranium. Their model treats proton and neutron densities with separate momentum scales. Asymmetric nuclei, where the two counts differ a lot, get special care. The scaling rules help experiments predict signals without a fresh heavy calculation for every target.
arxiv-2601-21473:
Zaifeng Pan and eight co-authors make large multi-agent simulations cheaper to run. Simulations where each agent is a language model are spreading across many fields. Each agent keeps private state on the graphics chip, and memory fills fast as the agent count grows.

The authors notice two helpful traits of these workloads. Only a few agents are active at any moment, and the order of future calls can be estimated. Their system, ScaleSim, manages memory based on how soon each agent will be called next. That foresight keeps the chip from choking as simulations scale up.
arxiv-2601-21573:
Masaki Miyashita studies how a firm should spread its products across features that buyers care about. The work builds on a hedonic model where a single representative buyer values product characteristics. A monopolist selling several products chooses where each one sits in feature space.

The striking result is that the monopolist's choice matches the social planner's optimum. That holds even though the firm produces too little overall. In other words, the range of products is right even when the volume is wrong. The finding separates two questions policy often mixes: variety can be fine while quantity is the true distortion.
arxiv-2601-21673:
Dexuan Ding and eight co-authors compress brain scans into compact surrogates for Alzheimer's classification. Structural MRI is widely used to spot the disease. Most learning methods use heavy three-dimensional networks, slice-by-slice features, or frozen features from general image models.

Each route has costs in compute or in fit to the task. The authors build multimodal visual surrogates that summarize the scans more directly. A compact summary could make scan-based screening faster and cheaper to deploy. It may also travel better across hospitals, where scanner types and image quality vary a lot.
arxiv-2601-21873:
Jinhang Chai, Xuyuan Liu, Elynn Chen, and Yujun Yan study transfer learning for structured matrices. Learning systems often grow over time: new features arrive and internal representations expand into larger spaces. Earlier representations end up embedded inside bigger ones, with only limited new structure added.

The team studies how to transfer an estimate from a well-solved source task to a larger target task. Their matrices combine a low-rank part, which holds the main pattern, with a sparse part for exceptions. The 2026 preprint develops theory for this transfer as both the ambient dimension and the inner representation grow. Such results guide fields like recommendation and imaging, where models are retrained on ever wider data.
arxiv-2601-21973:
Erin Dawson extends a counting theory in tropical geometry. Tropical Tevelev degrees arise from maps between tropical moduli spaces of curves, counting how curves meet given conditions in a simplified, combinatorial version of geometry. Dawson and Cavalieri defined and computed these degrees in one specific case.

That case used a particular relation between the degree of the maps and the genus of the curves, with a fixed count of marked points. Dawson's 2026 preprint adds a new integer parameter to the theory, widening the family of degrees that can be defined and studied. Tropical counts often mirror classical algebraic geometry results, so each extension enlarges a dictionary between combinatorics and geometry.
arxiv-2601-22773:
Sung Une Lee and a team give builders a reusable template for safety cases for AI systems. A safety case is a structured argument that a system is safe enough. Their 2026 preprint notes that classic cases, from aviation and nuclear work, assume fixed bounds and known failure modes.

Modern AI breaks those assumptions: it shifts, learns, and acts on its own. Their template framework adapts the case form to that reality. Reusable parts can lift the floor for AI governance. The work serves regulators and builders alike. It turns a craft into a kit.
arxiv-2601-23173:
Chris Sherlock, Andrew Golightly, and Anthony Lee fix a failure mode in particle filtering for hidden Markov models. Sometimes every simulated particle scores zero likelihood for an observation, so the filter collapses. Then the filtering distribution cannot be estimated and the parameter likelihood reads zero.

Their partially alive scheme, nicknamed the Frankenfilter, keeps such runs going in a principled way. It slots into particle Metropolis-Hastings, a standard inference method. Robust filters matter for tracking, epidemiology, and finance, where zero-likelihood steps occur in real data. Partially alive particles keep the filter estimable through stretches where a naive particle set would collapse to zero.
arxiv-2603-02373:
Taylor Daniels studies signed partition numbers in this 2026 mathematics paper. Partitions split a whole number into a sum of smaller parts. Signed versions weight each part by a function that returns zero, one, or minus one. Daniels uses the Legendre symbol, a classic sign from number theory, as that weight.

Series formulas in the style of Rademacher are derived for several small primes. The primes covered are five, thirteen, and seventeen, all one more than a multiple of four. Derivations make clear how the method extends to all such primes. For the prime seventeen, deeper tools enter, including Dedekind sums and their twisted versions. The signed counts turn out to vanish exactly on certain arithmetic progressions modulo thirty-four.
arxiv-2603-02473:
Boqin Yuan, Yue Su, and Kun Yao diagnose where memory-augmented agents fail in this 2026 paper. Such agents store past interactions and retrieve them to answer later questions. Teams debate whether better writing or better retrieval matters more. Their diagnostic framework crosses three write styles with three retrieval methods.

Write styles range from raw chunks to extracted facts and summaries. Retrieval spans cosine matching, keyword search, and a hybrid reranker. On a long-conversation benchmark, retrieval choice swung accuracy by about twenty points. Write style moved it by only a few points. Raw chunks, needing no model calls, matched or beat costly lossy options. Failures clustered at retrieval, not at use of retrieved text. Better retrieval, they argue, beats fancier writing today.
arxiv-2603-02573:
Jiahao Lu, Jiayi Xu, Wenbo Hu, and colleagues track every pixel in 3D from a single video in this 2026 paper. Knowing each pixel's 3D path unlocks full understanding of video dynamics. Prior methods track only sparse points or rely on slow per-video optimization. Their feedforward model, Track4World, aims for dense tracking at practical speed.

A transformer first encodes the global 3D scene from the video. A novel 3D correlation scheme then estimates dense 2D and 3D flow between any frame pair. Scene flow plus rebuilt geometry yields the 3D trajectory of every pixel. Tracking happens in world coordinates, not camera coordinates, which suits reconstruction. Across multiple benchmarks, the method beat existing approaches on flow and tracking. Robustness and scale suit real-world four-dimensional reconstruction tasks.
arxiv-2603-02673:
Baptiste Ferrere, Nicolas Bousquet, Fabrice Gamboa, and colleagues solve a long-standing gap in model explanation math. Their 2026 paper concerns functional ANOVA, which splits a model's output into single-feature effects and interactions between features. For linked categorical features, no exact formula existed, so teams relied on slow sampling estimates.

By linking the problem to an extended form of discrete Fourier analysis, they derive a closed-form split that assumes nothing about the links. The formula is fast to compute and reduces to the classic result when features are independent. It also yields a natural extension of SHAP values, a popular explanation score, to the general categorical case. Exact answers replace rough estimates for a wide class of models.
arxiv-2603-02773:
Zhen Zhang, Zihan Wang, Xinyu Ma, and colleagues help search models absorb new documents without full retraining. Their 2026 paper concerns generative retrieval, where a model answers a query by generating a document's ID directly. Such models often fail on documents added after training, and retraining is costly and can erase old skill.

Their method, DOME, edits the model in three stages: find the key layers, tune edit vectors, then apply the update. A mixed-label training trick keeps edit vectors distinct even when documents share ID parts across queries. On the NQ and MS MARCO benchmarks, new-document retrieval improved a lot while old results held. The update took only about sixty percent of the time of incremental retraining.
arxiv-2603-02873:
Tianyou Liu, Ziqiang Li, Xurui Liu, and colleagues argue that the TeX typesetting system holds back AI-assisted science writing. Their 2026 paper examines LaTeX compilation in an era when language models draft much of the text. They cite slow builds, weak meaning in the output, hard-to-locate errors, and a costly token footprint.

As an alternative they present Mogan STEM, a structured editor that shows the document as it will look while editing. Tests favor Mogan on build and rendering time and on language model task performance. Its file format also carries less redundant information, making model fine-tuning cheaper than with TeX files. The authors call for larger trials of training models on the new format.
arxiv-2603-03173:
Hassan Abdelraouf and Jeff Shamma ask whether choosing the wrong good learning rule can itself be a mistake. No-regret algorithms guarantee that, over time, a learner does about as well as the best fixed strategy. Yet that promise says nothing about how high the final average actually is, and different no-regret rules can land at different heights.

Framing generalized replicator dynamics as control systems, they compare variants by reshaping one internal block. Near equilibrium, a passivity test ranks the variants. Globally, an anticipatory variant provably dominates the standard rule across every payoff environment, with an optimal-control argument showing the reward gap can reach zero. A genuine free lunch exists among no-regret dynamics, at least in this family.
