gao-gaoreports-gao-05-873: Medicare contracting reform had gaps in 2005, and GAO's report says CMS's plan was incomplete and anticipated savings were uncertain. The findings demand the fixes. The report warns that the seniors' program deserved honest math. The gaps had to be closed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-273: The internet tax moratorium's revenue impacts varied in 2006, and GAO's report says the effects would differ by state. The findings do the math. The report warns that the online tax holiday had uneven costs. The impacts had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-473: Missile defense planning needed better cost visibility in 2006, and GAO's report says actions were required to improve operational planning and cost tracking. The findings demand the transparency. The report warns that the shield's billions deserved honest accounting. The costs had to be visible.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-73: D.C. charter school closures needed better handling in 2005, and GAO's report says strengthening monitoring and process could ease the transitions. The findings demand the care. The report warns that the students deserved orderly closures. The monitoring had to be stronger.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-973: FAA funding options got a GAO look in 2006, and the report offers observations on potential funding paths. The findings lay out the choices. The report asks who should pay for the skies of tomorrow. The options had to be weighed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-273: Open-ended Pentagon deals were bleeding in 2007 — GAO's report says time-and-materials contracts needed better insight and controls. The findings target the blank-check corner of defense buying. The report's fix: watch the clock, cap the meter, and stop paying by the shrug.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-373: Bad nursing homes needed better targeting in 2007 — GAO's report says federal helpers should aim aid where the care was worst. The findings demand smarter triage of the quality-improvement money. The report's cause: the frailest patients deserve the sharpest oversight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-573: Food stamp sign-ups were stuck in the paper age in 2007 — GAO's report says easier application methods could use a real boost. The findings press for modernization of the process. The report's logic is humane: hunger should not require a fax machine.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-673: Tax season 2007 was a stress test for the IRS — GAO's report gives the interim filing-season results and grades the 2008 budget ask. The findings link performance to funding in detail. The report's question: did the agency earn the dollars it wanted?
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-73: This 2007 GAO report presses the nuclear weapons labs to prove their safety push is real. The labs that build and tend the nation's bombs had launched fix-up drives for both bomb work and staff safety — but GAO found no hard proof the drives worked. The report demands facts, not pledges, from the most dangerous workshops in the land.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-773: The Government Accountability Office dug into human Capital: DOD Needs to Improve Implementation of and Address Employee Concerns about Its National Security Personnel System in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Th:
On the morning of September 11, 1973, CIA officers briefed President Richard Nixon on the military coup then unfolding in Chile. That top secret President's Daily Brief stayed classified for fifty years. The National Security Archive posted it in August 2023, in a briefing book edited by Peter Kornbluh.

The brief told Nixon that Chilean officers were determined to restore political and economic order. It also warned that they might lack a coordinated plan to use the wide civilian opposition. Reading it shows exactly what the president was told, in the CIA's own words, on the day Salvador Allende fell.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_henry-ki: Kissinger Told Soviet Envoy during 1973 Arab-Israeli War: the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
hodge-systematic-theology-vol3-1873:
Volume three of Hodge's Systematic Theology, in this 1874 edition, crowns the Princeton system with eschatology, the doctrine of the last things. Hodge had covered God, man, and Christ's work in the earlier volumes. The aged professor writes here with a lifetime of teaching behind him.

He treats death, the soul's state after death, the return of Christ, resurrection, and the final judgment in ordered sequence. His method stays the same: gather the Bible's statements, sort them, and answer rival views with calm reason. Princeton's students received the volume as the completion of the great Calvinist system in America.
human-science-or-phrenology-its-principl: Human Science, or Phrenology, 1873. The human science. This book preserves that work. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Kept for study.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lucas-louis-art:
Louis Arthur Lucas (1851–1876) was an African explorer born in London, profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind. After travel in the United States and Egypt, he organized an expedition to explore the Kongo. He reached Khartum in January 1876 and died at sea that November, aged twenty-five.

At the Albert Nyanza, Lucas navigated the lake’s northern part in the first steamboat ever launched on it, working alongside Colonel Gordon. He also compiled a vocabulary of Bisharin words, later published by the Anthropological Institute. Against Gordon’s advice he then tried to cross Africa, fell sick and paralyzed, and died on a steamboat between Suakim and Suez. He was buried at Jiddah. The entry tells a short, stark story of ambition, illness, and an early death in the age of exploration.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magnus-lady-kat:
Lady Katie Magnus, an English author and communal worker, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Portsmouth on May 2, 1844, she was the daughter of E. Emanuel. She married Sir Philip Magnus. Her public life joined writing to service in London's Jewish community.

The article lists her books and her posts together. She served on committees of the Berkeley Street Synagogue and backed the Jews' Deaf and Dumb Home. As treasurer of the Jewish Girls' Club she worked for young women. Her writing began with Bible stories and holiday tales for children. Two sketches of Jewish history followed, one reaching three editions. Her Outlines of Jewish History was reprinted in America by the Jewish Publication Society. A second edition of her Jewish Portraits appeared in 1901. The entry shows a writer who taught her community its own past.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manoah-b-jacob-:
Manoah ben Jacob, a French Talmudist of Lunel, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He lived in the second half of the thirteenth century. After a short stay at Narbonne, where he studied with Meir ben Simon and Reuben ben Hayyim, he returned to Lunel. He often cites rulings in his father's name.

The article centers on his one known work. Like several of his contemporaries, Manoah studied Maimonides closely. He wrote a commentary on the Yad ha-Hazakah, Maimonides' great code. Later writers quote it under the title Sefer ha-Manoah, or Sefer ha-Menuhah. It was printed at Constantinople in 1518, centuries after his death. The entry rests on the standard name-books of Azulai and Conforte and on Gross's Gallia Judaica. It preserves a Provençal scholar who helped France read Maimonides.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-matah-mehasya-m:
Matah Mehasya was a town in southern Babylonia. Solomon Schechter and Wilhelm Bacher untangle it from its neighbor Sura in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. Sherira Gaon used the two names as if they were one place, since both named the seat of the great academy founded by Rab. The article argues from Talmudic passages, including one that contrasts the two towns' ways of speaking, that they were really separate towns. The school likely sat between them.

Most of the entry belongs to the age of Ashi, in the later fourth century. The academy then sat at Matah Mehasya, and Ashi himself lived there. He protected the town by forbidding houses taller than its synagogue. He also complained that its non-Jewish residents stayed hard-hearted. They saw the splendor of the Torah at the great Kallah gatherings twice a year, and still stayed unmoved.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ben-isaac-:
Meir ben Isaac of Orleans, a French liturgical poet of the end of the eleventh century, is entered in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn. He and his son Eleazar are quoted in a commentary on Chronicles that was wrongly ascribed to Rashi, and the entry floats the possibility that Meir himself wrote biblical commentary. His certain work is poetry for the synagogue, signed in acrostics that spell the name Eleazar, apparently for his son.

Two poems are singled out. "Torah ha-Temimah" is a supplication woven with Aramaic and Talmudic phrases, expressing his horror of apostasy. "Almanot Hayyot" is a penitential prayer for the Day of Atonement, which Zunz translated into German. A third penitential poem, on a Crusader massacre of three thousand Jews, carries the same signature, but Zunz judged it a work of a century later.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendes-nasi-fra:
Francisco Mendes-Nasi, head of a great Lisbon banking house and husband of the famous Gracia, is noticed in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling. One of the richest and most respected Portuguese Marranos, he died about 1536; his bank, with branches in Flanders and France, advanced money to Charles V and other rulers. His brother Diogo, who ran the Antwerp branch, succeeded him as the richest Portuguese Marrano, and with his sister-in-law spent great sums trying to keep the Inquisition out of Portugal.

The entry ends with a kinsman's repartee. Hector Mendes, a very rich man, was asked by the King of Portugal what he called his own, and answered: "The alms which I have given." The notice is short, but it sketches the banking dynasty into which Beatrice de Luna married and which she would soon lead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mezey-franz-107:
Franz Mezey, born at Acsad in Hungary on February 5, 1860, was a jurist who became the organizational backbone of Hungarian Jewry. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. Destined by his parents for the rabbinate, he mastered Hebrew, then chose law and was admitted to the Budapest bar.

In 1883 Mezey was a mainstay of the defense in the Tisza-Eszlár blood accusation case, acting for Hungary's Jews. As secretary of the national Jewish chancery for twenty years, he drove progress in religious and school affairs. He co-founded the Hungarian Jewish Literary Society, edited journals with Bacher and Blau, and ran Budapest's burial society, grown to 10,000 members under him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mires-jules-isa:
Jules Isaac Mirès, born at Bordeaux on December 9, 1809, was the French financier who built a railway-and-press empire and twice stood convicted. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. A broker in 1848, he took over the Arles gas company after the February Revolution and moved into newspapers.

With Millaud he ran the Journal des Chemins de Fer and organized its investment fund, and by 1851 he owned Le Pays and Le Constitutionnel as well. At Marseilles he built a harbor, a new quarter, and gas lighting, and in 1860 he won the Roman railways concession. A five-year prison sentence in 1861 was overturned on appeal, though a pamphlet attacking his judges earned him six months in 1869.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monzon-abraham-:
Abraham Monzon the Elder, a rabbi of the later sixteenth century who died at Constantinople, was called by his contemporaries Sinai we-Oḳer Harim — an encyclopedia, and an uprooter of mountains. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Meyer Kayserling give him his Jewish Encyclopedia notice in 1906. A pupil of Bezaleel Ashkenazi, he served first as rabbi in Egypt.

He was also a fine scribe whose Torah scrolls were still extant in Egypt centuries later. His decisions and responsa survive scattered through the great collections — Samuel of Medina's, Solomon Cohen's, Abraham de Boton's, Joseph di Trani's. Still in manuscript when the entry was written were more responsa, novellae, sermons, and a defense of Ḥayyim Vital against Menahem di Lonsano.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ha-darsha:
Moses ha-Darshan was a French Bible exegete who headed the yeshiva of Narbonne in the middle eleventh century. Wilhelm Bacher and Max Schloessinger wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He came from a Narbonne family long distinguished for learning. His name means Moses the expounder of Scripture.

With Tobiah ben Eliezer, Moses was the leading voice of midrashic, symbolic reading of the Bible in his century. His book, perhaps called Yesod, is lost and known mainly from quotations in Rashi. It mixed older haggadah with ideas of his own, some touched by Christian thought, which may be why it perished. Its echoes live on in later midrashim, and his pupils included Nathan ben Jehiel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mosse-benjamin-:
Benjamin Mosse was rabbi of Avignon, born at Nimes on December 8, 1832. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He founded the monthly periodical La Famille de Jacob. He died at Marseilles on July 24, 1892, after a life of writing for French Jews.

His books range wide: poems, a work on the rights and duties of man that ran through fourteen editions, and a civic instruction manual. He wrote on the women of Jewish antiquity and on Dom Pedro the Second of Brazil. He also made a literal, line-by-line translation of the Psalms, with a grammar before it. In 1884 he translated Abravanel's Rosh Amanah into French.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neumann-salomon:
Salomon Neumann was a German doctor and maker of statistics. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Pyritz, Pomerania, on Oct. 22, 1819. He studied medicine at Berlin and at Halle. He took his degree in 1842.

Neumann practiced as a doctor in Berlin from 1845. In 1875 he received the title Sanitätsrat. His essays filled many medical journals of the day. His first book treated public health care and property. He wrote on the Berlin census of 1861. He wrote, too, on Berlin's syphilis question. His fame rests most on his use of numbers. He aimed statistics at the claims of anti-Semitic writers. His 1880 book attacked the mass-immigration fable directly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-noah-mordecai-m:
Mordecai Manuel Noah was an American Jewish public man. Cyrus Adler and Max Raisin wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Philadelphia in 1785. He died in New York city in 1851. Orphaned early, he was apprenticed to a carver.

Schooling came to him a few hours each day. Evenings went to the theater and the Franklin Library. Law study took him to Charleston as an editor. War articles under a pen name made him enemies. In 1813 he became consul to Tunis. He freed twelve enslaved American sailors there credibly. Overspending his allowance let opponents force his recall. Monroe's letter blamed his Jewish faith for it. Sheriff, judge, and port surveyor followed at home. His plays made him America's most popular playwright then. In 1825 he planned a Jewish city, Ararat.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ohalot-tents-11:
Ohalot, which means Tents, is a tract of the Mishnah. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It deals with uncleanness from a dead human body. It also deals with dead beasts and with sick touch. Its base text is a passage in the book of Numbers.

Ohalot is the second tract in the order called Tohorot. That order treats rules of clean and unclean things. The tract holds eighteen chapters in all. It holds one hundred and thirty-three parts as well. The first part lists kinds of uncleanness from the dead. It counts the parts of the human body at 248. Later parts treat flesh, bones, blood, and ash. They ask how much of each can make a man unclean.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ornstein-abraha:
Abraham Philip Ornstein was an English rabbi and school man. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in London in the year 1836. He died at Cape Town on December 6, 1895. At first he taught at the Jews' Free School, London.

At eighteen Abraham became minister to the flock at Portsea. In 1860 he moved to Birmingham as a school head. He ran the Hebrew National Schools there for six years. He then took a call to Melbourne, in Australia. He held that post for ten full years there. In Melbourne he ran a paper called Australian Israel. He helped found and run the almshouses of that town. In 1882 he went to Cape Town for good. He led the flock there till the year 1895.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palm-phnix-dact:
The palm is a tree that stays green in hot, dry lands. Emil G. Hirsch and Gerson B. Levi wrote on it for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its word, tamar, is shared by three old tongues. Those tongues are Aramaic, Ethiopic, and Hebrew as well. The Arabic word tamr names the fruit more than the tree.

The date palm has a slim stem that bends in storms. It sways back and forth but does not break apart. Rings on its stem mark where old leaves fell off. A crown of fronds, forty to eighty in count, tops it. The fruit grows in that crown of green fronds. Some trees are male and some are female in kind. So men must spread the dust of one to the next. Its fruit turns from green to gold, then to dark.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pecs-funfkirche:
Pecs, also called Fünfkirchen, is a royal free city in Hungary. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its first Jewish families came late in the eighteenth century. They held services in a rented room at first.

By 1835 some twenty families had formed a congregation. Growth led to a large new synagogue, dedicated in 1869. The congregation was Reform in style from early on. It used an organ and sermons in Hungarian. A school for its children opened in 1840. About two thousand Jews lived in the city then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinsk-12173:
Pinsk is a Russian city in the Minsk government. Three scholars shared its entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They were J. G. Lipman, Herman Rosenthal, and Benzion Eisenstadt. Jews lived in Pinsk before the year 1500. Its archive record runs long and detailed.

In 1506 the prince granted land for a synagogue. The same grant gave land for a cemetery too. It confirmed the Jews in their Lithuanian privileges. Queen Bona confirmed the grant again in 1533. Pinsk Jews traded in the market by the castle. Some owned land, farmed taxes, and held leases.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-rabbath-:
Rabbah, also called Rabbath, was the capital of the Ammonites. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. There the bed of the giant Og was shown to men. Deuteronomy tells of that vast iron bed. David laid siege to the city and took it. The tale stands in the second book of Samuel.

Under Solomon the city passed from Israel's hand again. Ammon won back its freedom at the kingdom's split. Rabbah grew great and rich once more in that age. Fine palaces rose inside its walls. The prophets spoke doom on it more than once. Amos and Jeremiah both name it as a hated foe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raphael-ben-jek:
Raphael ben Jekuthiel Süsskind ha-Kohen was a Talmudist born on November 4, 1722. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Bernhard Friedberg wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Livonia. He died at Altona on November 26, 1803.

The article lists rabbinates at Rakov, Vilkomir, Minsk, and Pinsk. In 1772 he became rabbi of Posen. Four years later he led the Three Communities near Hamburg. He served them for twenty three years before retiring. The King of Denmark thanked him in a letter. Raphael also fought hard against Mendelssohn and modern culture. The entry shows a strict leader held in high honor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reuchlin-johann:
Johann Reuchlin was a German humanist born on February 22, 1455. Gotthard Deutsch and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Pforzheim and died in 1522. He studied at Freiburg, Paris, and Basel.

The article credits him with bringing Greek and Hebrew study westward. He served dukes as companion, judge, and ambassador. Later he taught Greek and Hebrew at Ingolstadt and Tübingen. Pico di Mirandola first sparked his interest in Cabala. Jacob Loans taught him Hebrew from 1492. Obadiah of Sforno later taught him in Rome. His Bible work led him into Talmud study. The entry then turns to his fight with Pfefferkorn. That fight concerned the planned destruction of Hebrew books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rittangel-johan:
Johann Stephanus Rittangel was a German controversial writer who died in 1652. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Forscheim near Bamberg. He died at Königsberg.

The article reports a shifting religious path for him. He was born a Jew, it is stated. He then became Catholic, then Calvinist, then Lutheran. He taught Oriental languages at Königsberg. He translated the Sefer Yezirah in 1642. He translated the Passover Haggadah in 1644. One of the earliest translations of Jewish prayers was his. A posthumous work argues the Targums prove the Trinity. That claim was also the theme of another book. The entry follows a convert who argued from Jewish texts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rozsavolgyi-ros:
Markus Rózsavölgyi, born Rosenthal, was a Hungarian composer born at Balassa-Gyarmath in 1787. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. At eleven he went to Vienna to study music, drawn to Magyar song.

Rózsavölgyi built his works on Hungary's national music and themes. He became the most popular violinist of the century's first decade there. In 1812 he conducted the orchestra at Pesth's German Theater. His surname was publicly Magyarized to Rózsavölgyi in 1824. Famous Gypsy musicians of the age had been his pupils at Vienna and Pesth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sabsovich-hirsc:
Hirsch Leib Sabsovich was mayor of Woodbine, New Jersey, a Jewish farm colony. Cyrus Adler and J. G. Lipman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was born at Berdyansk, Russia, on February 25, 1860.

Sabsovich studied agriculture and farm chemistry at Odessa and at Zurich. In 1888 he emigrated to the United States for good. He worked as chemist at Colorado's experiment station for two years. From 1891 he advised the new Woodbine colony on its farming. He also ran its Baron de Hirsch school and served as borough mayor. He also served as secretary of the Cape May county board of agriculture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samson-ben-abra:
Samson ben Abraham of Sens was a French tosafist born about 1150. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Called the Prince of Sens, he studied under Rabbenu Tam at Troyes.

For ten years Samson attended Isaac ben Samuel's school at Dampierre. On that master's death he took charge of the school of Sens himself. Asheri ranks his influence on Talmud study next after Tam and Isaac. His tosafot, cut down by Eliezer of Touques, remain principal sources for reading the Talmud. He told questioners to reject his view if theirs differed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sandals-hebrew-:
Joseph Jacobs, Immanuel Benzinger, Wilhelm Bacher, and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on sandals. In the warm East, shoes matter less than in cold northern lands. Still, people in hilly Palestine did not go barefoot as often as Egyptians did. Bible verses suggest even the poor usually owned shoes. Many went barefoot at home and wore sandals for travel.

The Hebrew sandal was a simple sole tied on with straps. Sandals were made of leather, woven work, papyrus, or linen. Some had a bent-up front or a heel piece. Two straps crossed over the instep. A third, thinner strap passed between the great toe and the second toe. Men and women wore the same style. No shoes were worn indoors. The sanctuary was always entered barefoot. The article ends with rabbinic rules on sandal shapes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schiller-szines:
Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Solomon Mayer Schiller-Szinessy. He was reader in rabbinic at Cambridge University. Schiller-Szinessy was born at Alt-Ofen, in Hungary, in 1820. He died at Cambridge on March 11, 1890. He took his doctorate at Jena and was ordained a rabbi. He taught at the Lutheran College of Eperies.

In 1848 Schiller-Szinessy backed Hungary's revolution against Austria. He carried out the order to blow up the bridge at Szegedin. That blast checked the Austrian advance. Wounded and captured, he escaped the night before his execution. He reached Ireland, then London, then a pulpit at Manchester. In 1863 he moved to Cambridge. He catalogued the university's Hebrew manuscripts in 1876. The university made him its teacher of Talmud in 1866. It granted him a master's degree in 1878.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shibboleth-1357:
Shibboleth is a Hebrew word meaning flood, ear of corn, or branch. Emil G. Hirsch and S. Hecht wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. The word appears in several Bible passages with those senses. Its fame comes from one grim scene in Judges.

After beating Ephraim, the Gileadites held the Jordan fords. They stopped fleeing men and asked if they were Ephraimites. A man who said no faced one spoken test. Say Shibboleth, they demanded at the crossing. Ephraimites pronounced the first sound differently, as Sibboleth. That slip betrayed them to their deaths. The entry explains how a word for corn became history's best-known password test.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shma-asmodeus-a:
Aeshma, known in Jewish sources as Asmodeus or Ashmedai, was chief of the demons in the Mazdian faith. Erik Stave wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the figure. In the oldest Avesta texts he seems mostly an abstract idea. Later Avesta passages present him as a personal evil being.

Aeshma serves Angro-mainyush, the great spirit of evil. His foe is Sraoscha, one of the good angels of Ahuramazda. His special work is filling human hearts with anger and revenge. All evil in the world runs through his agency, believers held. He hardens men in evil and blocks the path of right. Whether lust defined him, as with Tobit's Asmodeus, stays undecided. The entry compares Persian and Jewish demon lore with care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-silveyra-miguel:
Miguel de Silveyra was a Spanish poet born at Celorico, Portugal, in the late sixteenth century. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He studied philosophy at Coimbra University in Portugal. Salamanca added law, medicine, and mathematics to his learning.

For twenty years Silveyra lectured at the Spanish court. He taught different sciences there, and poetry as well. Late in life he followed his patron to Naples. The duke of Medina de las Torres was that patron. At Naples his great heroic poem El Macabeo appeared in 1638. The poem celebrates the Maccabees in octave stanzas. Barrios counted Silveyra among the Jewish poets of Spain. Other critics doubt he ever professed Judaism at all. He died at Naples in 1638, the year his poem appeared.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-singer-isidore-:
Isidore Singer was an Austrian author and editor born in Moravia in 1859. Cyrus Adler and Frank H Vizetelly wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He founded the Jewish Encyclopedia itself. He studied at Vienna and Berlin, taking his degree in 1884. He then edited a literary journal in Vienna.

Singer later served a French ambassador and worked in Paris. There he founded La Vraie Parole to answer an anti-Semitic paper. In 1895 he went to New York to publish his encyclopedia. It first bore a longer title about Jewish history and thought. His many books dealt with antisemitism and the Jewish question in Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spitz-yom-tob-b:
Yom-Tob ben Isaac Spitz taught Hebrew and German at Prague. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He taught in the Jewish school of Prague for years. His time was the first half of the nineteenth century. His grandfather was Rabbi Eleazar Fleckeles of Prague.

He wrote Alon Bakut on his grandfather's death in 1826. His Zikron Eliezer gave a biography of Fleckeles in 1827. He also wrote a biography of his father, Isaac Spitz. He contributed sixteen scientific essays to Bikkure ha-Ittim, a Hebrew journal. Those essays appeared in volumes six and seven of that journal. The entry preserves a teacher's quiet literary career in brief.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-straus-ludwig-1:
Ludwig Straus was a Hungarian violinist born at Presburg on March 28, 1835. Isidore Singer and A. Porter wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied violin under Hellmesberger and Joseph Böhm. He also studied composition with Preyer and Nottebohm. His first public performance came at Vienna in 1850.

Straus toured widely and met the cellist Piatti in 1857. They concertized together through Germany and Sweden. In 1859 he led the opera orchestra at Frankfort. He settled in England in 1864 for good. There he played solo violin in the court orchestra. He conducted Philharmonic concerts in London and Manchester. He taught violin at the London Academy of Music until 1894. The entry charts a touring virtuoso turned London fixture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-suretyship-1337:
Suretyship is the pledge to answer for another person's debt. Wilhelm Bacher and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. The Pentateuch names a surety only once. In Genesis, Judah pledges himself for Benjamin's safe return. Proverbs returns to the theme again and again.

Proverbs warns often against standing surety for others. It also urges sureties to keep their word once given. The Hebrew word for pledge passed into Latin as arrabo. Talmud law splits sureties into two kinds. One joins the loan from the start as a party. The other, the kabbelan, takes the debt as his own. Modern law calls that figure an accommodation maker. The entry maps an old contract idea onto modern terms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-szanto-emil-141:
Emil Szanto was an Austrian philologist born at Vienna in 1857. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born on November 22, son of Simon Szanto. He studied at the University of Vienna. He died there on December 14, 1904.

Szanto became a lecturer at Vienna in 1884. He rose to professor of Greek history and archaeology in 1898. Greek inscriptions were his ruling specialty. His books study Athenian citizenship rights in depth. Others treat Greek state loans and mortgage law. A travel volume reports his journey in Caria. He also revised a handbook of Greek antiquities. The entry records a short life spent on Greek stones and laws.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tax-gatherers-1:
Tax-gatherers farmed the revenues of cities under foreign rule. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Under Egypt, each city's taxes went to the highest bidder yearly. The farmer paid the treasury a fixed sum. Any surplus above it was his own gain.

Under Ptolemy the Fourth, Joseph ben Tobiah leased whole regions. Coele-Syria, Phoenicia, and Judea all fell under his lease. He held the collector's office for twenty-two years. His son Hyrcanus succeeded him in the post. Rents doubled from 8,000 to 16,000 talents meanwhile. Both men still amassed immense riches. Joseph beheaded twenty citizens who refused their taxes. Toward fellow Jews, though, father and son showed leniency. The entry shows tax farming as power and peril.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-thomas-emile-em:
Emile Thomas, born Emil Tobias, was a German actor born at Berlin in 1836. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He debuted in 1852 with a touring company in Saxony. For three years the troupe paid him in food alone.

Engagements followed at Görlitz, Leipsic, Cologne, and Breslau. A Berlin director spotted him and made him stage-manager. He staged Offenbach and led Hamburg's Thalia Theater for nine years. Later he managed theaters in Berlin and toured as a star. An American tour in 1886 brought money and praise. His own Thomas-Theater venture failed, though. He kept acting in Germany and Austria afterward.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-traditions-1447: Traditions are doctrines and sayings passed by word of mouth from father to son. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Such traditions form a large part of Jewish oral teaching. Many legal doctrines trace their line back to Moses at Sinai. Other traditions concern national and historical events instead. One holds that Amoz, Isaiah's father, and King Amaziah were brothers. Another says the Holy of Holies stood outside the Temple's set measure. Hebrew calls tradition Masoret or Kabbalah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ulmann-albert-1:
Albert Ulmann was an American banker and author born in New York in 1861. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Public schools and City College gave him his education. In 1900 he joined a New York Stock Exchange firm. He helped found the Judaeans society and served as governor.

New York history and its Jews drew his keen interest. He wrote for the New York Times Saturday Review. The Saturday Evening Post also carried his work. His first book, Frederick Struther's Romance, appeared in 1889. Chaperoned followed in 1894 as a second novel. A Landmark History of New York came in 1901. Another volume cataloged the city's historical sites and tablets.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-verblovski-greg:
Gregori Leontyevich Verblovski was a Russian jurist. Herman Rosenthal and Vasili Rosenthal wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Verblovski died at Moscow in 1900. He studied law at the University of St. Petersburg. He graduated from there in 1866. He then served as a court secretary and judge.

His books collect and explain Russian court rulings. His first set covers civil court decisions from 1866 to 1875. Later sets carry the series through 1888. He also wrote on how a Russian civil lawsuit proceeds. Other works treat tax law and railway rules. The entry lists a long shelf of practical legal guides.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wandering-jew-1:
The Wandering Jew is a figure from Christian legend. Joseph Jacobs wrote this long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The tale tells of a Jerusalem shoemaker. He taunted Jesus on the way to the cross. Jesus told him to go on forever until his return. The legend first appeared in print in 1602.

The first pamphlet named the wanderer Ahasverus. Eight editions appeared in Germany in that first year. Forty more followed by 1800. The story spread to France, England, Denmark, and Sweden. Reports claimed sightings from Hamburg to Paris. Claims of a living witness to the crucifixion fed the tale. The entry tracks each version and appearance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wessely-moritz-:
Moritz August Wessely was a German doctor. He was born at Bleicherode on October 15, 1800. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died at Nordhausen on March 7, 1850. He was a nephew of Naphtali Hirz Wessely. He studied at Halle and Göttingen.

Wessely took his medical degree in 1823. He then studied in Paris for five years. In 1828 he settled at Nordhausen to practice. He practiced there until his death. The Duke of Nassau gave him a privy title. Prussia's king named him a health councilor. In 1849 he founded two medical journals. He edited both journals until he died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolf-adolph-gra:
Adolph Grant Wolf (born 1869) was an American lawyer who rose to a high court post. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Washington, he took degrees at Johns Hopkins. He then earned law degrees at a Washington law school.

He joined the bar in 1893. Next he took more study at the University of Berlin. Back in Washington, he worked for the United Hebrew Charities. He served there as financial secretary from 1895. In 1902 he won a seat as a judge. The post was on the Supreme Court of Porto Rico. The short entry traces a fast rise in law. It links city charity work with a federal court role.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yehudai-ben-nah:
Yehudai ben Nahman, known as Yehudai Gaon, led the Sura school for four years. Isidore Singer and Max Schloessinger wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He held that post from 760 to 764 of this era. His rise broke with the old way of choice.

The exilarch passed over the men of Sura at that time. He chose a man of the Pumbedita school in his place. Soon after, the man's brother took the Pumbedita chair. Yehudai was blind in both of his eyes then. Some hold he was blind when he won the post. That fact cuts against a Talmud rule on blind judges. Yet Yehudai held that a blind man could lead prayer. His word on the law was held in high awe for ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zarfati-15173:
Zarfati names an east Jewish family traced back to France. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A book man traced the line to the kin of Rashi. That line runs through his grandson Rabbenu Tam of France.

The entry names five men of the line in brief. Elijah Zarfati was chief rabbi of Fez near 1770. Joseph Zarfati was a Turk scholar of the early 1600s. His book of sermons bears the name Yad Yosef in print. Samuel Zarfati was chief rabbi of Fez in the 1700s. He wrote a work in defense of the views of Maimonides. Two men named Vidal held the Fez post in past years. One wrote a work on the Talmud with a sweet name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zirndorf-heinri:
Heinrich Zirndorf was a German poet and rabbinical scholar who ended his career in America. Isidore Singer and M. Zametkin wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Fürth, Bavaria, on May 7, 1829, he died in Cincinnati on December 17, 1893. His parents planned a business career for him, but poetry pulled him toward study.

After years in Munich, Vienna, Hungary, and London, Zirndorf taught in Münster and then took a pulpit in Detroit. In 1884 he became professor of history at Hebrew Union College in Cincinnati. His works include the tragedy Kassandra, a volume of poems, and a book on Isaac Marcus Jost and his friends. A set of his sketches appeared in English as Some Jewish Women.
junctinus-speculum-astrologiae-1573:
Francesco Giuntini, known in Latin as Junctinus, was a Florentine Carmelite and astrologer to great houses. His Speculum Astrologiae, Mirror of Astrology, appeared in 1573. The massive commentary treats the casting and judgment of nativities, the birth charts on which the art staked its fame.

Junctinus gathers the rules of Ptolemy, the Arab masters, and the Latin tradition into one vast storehouse for the working astrologer. Kings and courtiers of his age kept such men close, and his book shows the learning their favor bought. Scholars of Renaissance astrology still quarry the Speculum for the tradition it preserves entire. The sheer size of the work is part of its claim on the reader.
kant-critique-practical-reason-abbott-18:
Immanuel Kant published the Critique of Practical Reason in 1788, his main work on moral philosophy. The English text here is T. K. Abbott's translation of 1873. Kant argues that moral law comes from reason itself, not from desire or reward. His categorical imperative bids us act only on rules we could will for all.

Persons, for Kant, must always be treated as ends, never merely as means. He links morality to freedom and to belief in God and immortality as hopes of reason. The book founded a major school of ethics centered on duty. Its claims still anchor debates in moral philosophy today.
kant-groundwork-abbott-1873:
Immanuel Kant published his Groundwork on morals in 1785, here under the title Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals. The English text is T. K. Abbott's translation of 1873. Kant seeks the supreme rule of morality in reason alone. Good will, he says, is the only thing good without limit.

He states the categorical imperative in several forms for clarity. Act only on maxims fit to be universal law, and treat humanity always as an end. Shorter and clearer than the Critiques, the Groundwork is widely taught. It is the classic statement of duty-based ethics. Students of philosophy still meet Kant first through these pages.
maxwell-treatise-electricity-magnetism-v:
James Clerk Maxwell published Volume 1 of A Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism in 1873. Maxwell, a Scottish physicist at Cambridge, set out to present the whole science in mathematical form. Volume 1 treats electrostatics and electrokinematics, the study of steady currents.

Maxwell defined electric charge, potential, and capacitance with care and built the math his theory needed. He wrote for students who would work problems, not just admire results. The famous equations take their full form in the second volume, but the first lays every tool they use. The Treatise began the mathematical unification of electricity and magnetism that changed physics and, in time, radio and all electrical technology.

Volume 2 of Maxwell's Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism appeared in 1873, completing the work. The second volume treats magnetism and electromagnetism, where Maxwell's own discoveries stand. It is here that his theory reaches the speed of light and names light itself an electromagnetic wave.

Maxwell showed that electric and magnetic disturbances travel at a fixed speed matching the measured speed of light. From that match he concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave, a claim Hertz later proved by experiment. The equations appear here in their original form, in components rather than modern vector shorthand. The volume is one of the great achievements of nineteenth-century science.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
Volume fourteen of Saint-Simon's memoirs opens at chapter one hundred five. A long war of words splits the King of England and his son. George has driven the Prince of Wales from the palace.

The King cut his son's income till he could barely subsist. Saint-Simon says the King did not believe the prince was his own. The Princess of Wales, full of sense and grace, softens the breach. Her court draws the most famed and trusted folk in England. Ministers feared her credit with the public and with Parliament. A royal family feud becomes state business in this telling.
mill-autobiography-1873:
John Stuart Mill's Autobiography appeared in 1873, the year of his death. Mill tells the story of his remarkable education under his father, James Mill. Greek at three and logic in childhood formed a mind of rare power. The book then recounts his mental crisis in his twenties, when dry analysis failed him.

Poetry, above all Wordsworth, restored his feelings and saved his life. Mill describes his growth toward a softer, wider utilitarianism. He also honors Harriet Taylor, his wife and intellectual partner. The book is the classic intellectual autobiography in English. It shows both the cost and the glory of a life of thought.
northern-nut-growers-association-report-:
Battle Creek, Michigan, hosted the tenth annual meeting of the Northern Nut Growers Association on December 9 and 10, 1919. This book reports the proceedings of that meeting. Like the sixth meeting's report, it opens with a long modern disclaimer. Member papers form the body of the book.

The disclaimer stresses that articles voice their authors alone. No product named is backed by the group, and none unnamed is slighted. Pesticide rules, it warns, have shifted since these talks were given. Growers must follow current label directions by law. Named nut kinds and growing methods may fail in other soils. The report preserves early American nut growing in detail.
openalex-w1794342673:
Albert Auguste, Scott Weaver, and co-authors studied this outbreak. Their paper appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2015. Fever with joint pain struck a Venezuelan village in 2010. The cause was Mayaro virus, a mosquito-borne alphavirus. Seventy-seven cases were reported in the outbreak.

Nineteen cases were confirmed by blood tests, they report. The virus was isolated from six sick patients. The team sequenced twenty-seven full virus genomes. Local strains belonged to genotype D, they found. A new genotype, called N, was also detected. The virus proved highly conserved across its range.
openalex-w2024037973:
Beverley Shea, Lex Bouter, Joan Peterson and colleagues tested a tool for judging systematic reviews. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2007. Thousands of health reviews have been published. Their quality varies a lot. The AMSTAR tool was built to appraise them. This study checked whether AMSTAR itself works well.

Two assessors applied AMSTAR to forty-two reviews. The reviews covered stomach acid related diseases. Other assessors gave each review a global quality rating. AMSTAR scores spread across a wide range. Different assessors mostly agreed on AMSTAR items. Total scores showed excellent agreement between assessors. AMSTAR results also matched the global ratings well. The authors concluded the tool is reliable for appraisal.
openalex-w2025773173:
Gary Weil, Will Kastens, Melinda Susapu and colleagues measured mass drug treatment for filariasis in Papua New Guinea. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2008. The Pacific's worst filariasis burden sits in that country. The disease comes from worms spread by mosquitoes.

Villages near Madang were studied before and after treatment rounds. Everyone was offered two drugs together, once a year. Three rounds were given under world health guidelines. Infection rates in blood fell sharply after three rounds. Signs of adult worms and worm antibodies also fell. Children showed the fastest drops of all. Worm DNA in local mosquitoes fell steeply too. The authors say follow-up must check if low levels rebound.
openalex-w2054711773:
Paul Martin and Estelle Martin-Granel traced the history of the word epidemic over twenty-five centuries. Their review appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2006. Homer first used the Greek word in a general sense. Hippocrates later gave it a medical meaning. Its sense has shifted many times since.

For Hippocrates, the word named a set of syndromes in one place. Medieval plagues narrowed the meaning. An epidemic became the spread of one clear disease. Germ science reshaped the term again in the nineteenth century. Its meaning shifted once more in recent decades. The authors expect further change ahead. Word history shows how medicine itself has changed.
openalex-w2162510673:
Evelyn Bromet, Laura Andrade, Irving Hwang, and colleagues published this study in BMC Medicine in 2011. They report the cross-national epidemiology of major depressive episodes from the World Mental Health Surveys. Depression ranks among the top causes of disability, yet basic data were missing for many countries, above all poorer ones.

Face-to-face interviews covered over eighty-nine thousand adults in eighteen countries. Lifetime rates ran higher in rich countries than in low- and middle-income ones, while recent rates were similar. Onset came in the mid-twenties on average, and women were affected about twice as often as men. Broken partnerships were the strongest social correlate. The authors tie depression firmly to social conditions everywhere.
openalex-w2168717473:
Luíz Trabulsi, Rogéria Keller, and Tânia Gomes published this synopsis in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2002. They contrast typical and atypical enteropathogenic Escherichia coli, gut bacteria that cause diarrhea. Typical strains lead infant diarrhea cases in developing countries but stay rare in rich nations, where atypical strains matter more.

The two types differ in several ways. Typical strains live only in humans, while atypical strains also live in animals. They differ in genes, surface types, and harm-causing traits as well. Atypical strains sit closer to the Shiga toxin producers, a dangerous E. coli group. The authors present atypical strains as emerging pathogens that health systems should watch more closely.
openalex-w2523258773:
Renata Nunes Oliveira, Maurício Cordeiro Mancini, and Fernando Cabral Salles de Oliveira studied natural wound-healing products in this 2016 paper. They tested five plant extracts sold in shops, including Brazilian and British propolis, pomegranate, dragon's blood, and sage. Such products are used on wounds partly to stop infection. The team measured their phenols and flavonoids, plant compounds tied to germ-killing and antioxidant action.

Infrared analysis, called FTIR, confirmed active compounds in every sample. Brazilian propolis held the most phenols, followed by pomegranate and the British kind. British propolis was richest in flavonoids, which the authors link to its origin. Pomegranate, British propolis, and dragon's blood showed the strongest antioxidant action. Every sample scored above eighty-two percent on that test. The results show which natural extracts carry the chemistry wanted for wound-care materials.
openalex-w2533504273:
G. Sybren de Hoog, Karolina Dukik, and Michel Monod led this taxonomy paper in Mycopathologia, published online in 2016. It proposes a new classification for dermatophytes, the fungi that infect skin, hair, and nails. The naming of these fungi had grown tangled over time. DNA family trees now offer a firmer basis for sorting them.

The team sequenced several genes from type and reference strains of the family Arthrodermataceae. The resulting trees largely agreed with each other and with earlier published trees. They showed the big genus Trichophyton was not one natural group. The paper therefore narrows Trichophyton and Microsporum and moves other species into Arthroderma, Lophophyton, and Nannizzia. It proposes one new genus and thirteen new name combinations. The scheme aims to give doctors and researchers stable, accurate fungal names.
openalex-w2802172273:
Francisco Tomás Gallo, Cynthia Katche, and Juan Facundo Morici, with colleagues, reviewed immediate early genes in Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience in 2018. These genes switch on within minutes when neurons fire during learning. Three of them, c-Fos, Egr1, and Arc, star in this review. Psychiatric disorders, despite their differences, share memory and thinking deficits.

Memory problems may be a shared trait running underneath many diagnoses, the authors note. Episodic and fear memories suffer in schizophrenia, depression, PTSD, and other conditions. Immediate early genes mark the neurons engaged as memories form and later reconsolidate. Tracking them reveals which circuits store which memories. Their dysregulation could link molecular events to psychiatric symptoms. The review connects gene-level neuroscience with the clinic. It argues memory machinery deserves more attention in how mental illness is understood.
openalex-w2910993873:
Kaustubh Adhikari, Javier Mendoza-Revilla, and Anood Sohail lead this genome-wide association study of pigmentation, in Nature Communications in 2019. Skin color lightens with distance from the equator, an adaptation to weaker sunlight. Europeans and East Asians lightened partly through different genes, suggesting convergent evolution. Latin Americans, with mixed ancestries, offer fresh ground for finding pigmentation loci.

The team scanned genomes of over six thousand Latin Americans for skin and eye pigmentation. They found eighteen association signals across twelve genomic regions. One locus, on chromosome ten, was new for skin pigmentation. Three more were new for eye pigmentation. Known regions near the TYR and OCA2 genes held multiple independent signals, plus interactions between loci. The results confirm that lighter skin evolved convergently in western and eastern Eurasia. Latin American genomes, the study shows, still hold undiscovered human variation.
openalex-w3080673473:
Andrey Chaves, Javad Azadani, Hussain Alsalman, and colleagues wrote this review in npj 2D Materials and Applications in 2020. It covers bandgap engineering in two-dimensional semiconductors, sheets of material a few atoms thick. The bandgap sets the colors of light a material absorbs and the voltages at which devices switch.

In these thin sheets, the bandgap changes with the number of layers in ways that break the usual textbook model. Stacking unlike sheets opens still more freedom, since no lattice matching is needed as in older layered devices. Twist angle and coupling between layers become design knobs of their own. The review gathers the physics and the experiments, showing how engineers can tune tomorrow's electronics and light sensors sheet by sheet.
openalex-w3155263273:
Wayne Holmes, Kaśka Porayska-Pomsta, Ken Holstein, and colleagues wrote this article for the International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, published online in 2021. It asks how researchers who build AI tools for learning should handle ethics. The authors argue that good intentions alone do not make a system fair or safe for students.

The team invited sixty leading researchers in the field to answer survey questions about ethics in education technology. Seventeen replied, and the paper sums up what they raised. Most had no training for the ethical questions now appearing. The authors call for a shared framework that joins expert guidelines with views from many fields. Such a framework, they argue, would help the field act with care.
openalex-w3202964273:
Laura Evans, Andrew Rhodes, Waleed Alhazzani, and colleagues present the 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines in Intensive Care Medicine. Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to infection, and septic shock is its most severe form. Hospitals worldwide need shared, current rules for spotting and treating both fast. These guidelines update earlier campaign advice for adult patients.

The panel recommends that hospitals run formal sepsis improvement programmes. These include screening acutely ill, high-risk patients and standard procedures for treatment. Each recommendation carries a strength rating and a note on the quality of its evidence. The aim is faster, more even care, so fewer patients die of a condition where hours matter.
openalex-w4213422773:
James Ratter, Samuel Bridgewater, and José Ribeiro compared the woody plants of Brazil's cerrado across hundreds of sites. Their paper appeared in the Edinburgh Journal of Botany in 2003. The cerrado is a vast savanna of trees and shrubs in central Brazil. This paper is the third in a series on its plant makeup. Knowing which species grow where underpins conservation of a fast-shrinking landscape.

The team analysed three hundred seventy-six areas of cerrado and Amazonian savanna. They recorded nine hundred fifty-one tree and large shrub species in total. About a third of those species appeared at only one site, showing strong local character. Computer clustering sorted the sites into regional groups, from the core cerrado to distinct Amazonian outliers.
openalex-w4220965973:
The LHCb collaboration reports a test of lepton universality in beauty-quark decays, in Nature Physics in 2022. The standard model of particle physics says electrons, muons, and taus should interact with identical strength. That sameness is called lepton universality. Earlier checks had mostly agreed with it, so any crack would be major news.

Using proton collision data from CERN's Large Hadron Collider, the team measured beauty mesons decaying to strange mesons plus electron or muon pairs. The rates did not match the predicted sameness. The mismatch reached a significance of just over three standard deviations. If later data confirm it, the result points to new physics, perhaps a new force between quarks and leptons.
openalex-w4283319873:
The One Health High-Level Expert Panel offers a new definition of One Health in PLOS Pathogens in 2022. One Health is the idea that human, animal, and environmental health form one linked system. The panel, shortened to OHHLEP, brings together experts advising world health and agriculture bodies. An opinion piece like this one carries weight because so many authorities stand behind it.

The panel argues that a clear, shared definition is needed for a sustainable and healthy future. Vague wording has let agencies pull in different directions during crises. A common definition should guide joint action on threats such as pandemics and food safety. The piece sets the wording that governments and agencies are urged to adopt.
openalex-w7202285173: Medical school grinds students down, but some bend without breaking. This study measured resilience among MBBS undergraduates and what correlated with it. The authors linked toughness to well-being. A medical-education study of the inner resources behind the white coat.
openalex-w7204938173: Why do some children struggle to learn to read or do math? This study looks to neuroscience for answers, examining how brain development in childhood relates to learning disorders and what that means for teaching. The authors review research on the mechanisms behind these difficulties and their classroom consequences. It bridges brain science and pedagogy, arguing that understanding the developing brain helps teachers reach struggling students.
openalex-w7206174973: Nurses in a hospital heart unit, where doctors thread thin tubes into patients' vessels, are expected to follow a set care process. This reflective article looks at how that process works in real life: what the evidence shows, what has improved, where the weak spots are, and what still needs work. It suggests ways to make steady, standard nursing care hold up in a fast, high-tech ward.
pare-deux-livres-chirurgie-1573:
Ambroise Pare, the great French surgeon of kings, brought out the first print of these two books of surgery in 1573. The text is in French, the tongue of his court and craft. Pare rose from a barber's shop to the chief surgeon's post of France.

The second book is his famed work on freaks and portents, Des monstres et prodiges. In it he sorts births of strange form, beasts of the land, and freaks of the sea. One part deals with sea freaks and the siren, and the book founds the learned study of such births.
plos-pbio-0020173:
David R. Halpin and Pehr B. Harbury launched a three-part methods series in PLOS Biology in 2004. The first paper sets out DNA display, a way to route large mixed pools of DNA based on their sequences. Each DNA strand acts as a label that directs where its attached cargo goes.

Sorting molecules by sequence could let chemists run many reactions in one pot and still keep track of each product. That is the base idea behind DNA-encoded libraries, now a major tool in drug hunting. Part one lays the routing rules. Later parts build genetic handling and synthesis on top of them. The series is a blueprint, best read as one project in three steps.
plos-pbio-0020273:
Miria Ricchetti, Fredj Tekaia, and Bernard Dujon traced stray DNA in the human genome in PLOS Biology in 2004. Mitochondria, the cell's power plants, have their own small genome. Over time, chunks of that DNA have leaked into the main genome in the nucleus, and the authors show the process has not stopped.

Fresh insertions can still be told apart from ancient ones by their condition. Recent arrivals look nearly intact, while old ones have decayed. That ongoing traffic means our genome is still being edited by its own power plants. It also creates a trap for researchers. A test for mitochondrial DNA may pick up a nuclear copy by mistake. That is a real concern in disease and ancestry studies.
plos-pone-0000073:
Esther Clarke, Ulrich H. Reichard, and Klaus Zuberbühler analyzed wild gibbon songs in PLOS ONE in 2006. Gibbons sing long, patterned duets at dawn. The authors broke those songs into units and asked whether the units combine by rules, like a simple syntax, and carry meaning for listeners.

Certain unit orders appeared again and again, and songs changed with context, such as the presence of a predator. Patterned rules plus context-linked change are two marks of a language-like system. Gibbon song will not be mistaken for speech, but it shows building blocks of it in our ape kin. That makes these songs a useful test case for how language could have evolved.
plos-pone-0000173:
Pedram Sendi, Huldrych F. Günthard, Mathew Simcock, and colleagues published this health economics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. When HIV treatment fails, doctors can order genotypic resistance testing, a lab test that reads the virus's genes to find drugs it still fears. The authors weigh whether that testing is cost-effective for patients whose therapy has failed.

Resistance tests cost money up front but can steer patients to drugs that work. The authors model the balance of cost and benefit. Their analysis helps clinics and insurers decide when testing pays for itself, a practical question in HIV care where second-line drugs are far more expensive.
plos-pone-0000273:
Aswin Sai Narain Seshasayee published this microbiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. DNA adenine methyltransferase, Dam for short, stamps chemical marks on E. coli DNA. The author assesses the enzyme's role in regulating gene expression, testing how much of the bacterium's gene control actually runs through this one methylating enzyme.

Dam methylation was known to affect a handful of E. coli processes, from DNA copying to virulence in relatives. A genome-wide assessment separates its broad effects from its minor ones. The paper helps settle how central this chemical marking system is to a model bacterium's daily life.
plos-pone-0000373:
Carmen Capone and co-authors investigated cell therapy for stroke damage in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. They worked with cells grown from neurospheres, small balls of neural stem-like cells raised in the lab. The question was whether these cells can protect the brain after blood flow is blocked, the event known as ischemia.

Rather than replacing lost brain cells, the transplanted cells appear to protect by changing the damaged tissue around them, the ischemic microenvironment. That shift in thinking matters for therapy design: a cell treatment might help mainly by calming harmful conditions near the injury. The study adds to efforts to turn stem cell science into stroke treatments.
plos-pone-0000473:
Claudio Lunardi and colleagues linked antibodies against a common virus to blood vessel damage, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Human cytomegalovirus infects most adults quietly and stays for life. The team found that a subset of antibodies against it can activate endothelial cells. These cells line the blood vessels. The antibodies can also push them toward apoptosis, programmed death.

Injured vessel lining is an early step in atherosclerosis, the artery disease behind heart attacks and strokes. If antiviral antibodies cross-react with the vessel wall, a lifelong infection could quietly raise cardiovascular risk. The authors draw that relevance explicitly, proposing one route by which chronic infection may feed chronic disease.
plos-pone-0000573:
Melissa A. Fowler and colleagues mapped two channels' presence across the rodent brain's emotion circuits, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The channels are TRPC4 and TRPC5, which let ions into neurons and shape their firing. The team charted corticolimbic expression of both channels, in cortex and limbic areas that process emotion and memory.

An expression map tells researchers which circuits a channel could influence, from fear to reward. TRPC channels have been tied to anxiety-like behavior in animals, making their addresses relevant to drug hunting. Mapping studies like this precede any claim that blocking a channel would help the brain rather than harm it.
plos-pone-0000673:
Dominique Lévesque, Francis P. Brière and Jean-Pierre Perreault described a modern way of switching on nucleic acid enzymes, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Enzymes evolved subtle activation modes to keep their targeting precise, as modern cell metabolism demands. One mode uses a target-dependent module, a docking domain that engages only when the right target appears. Such modules appear in small interfering RNAs and other systems.

Nucleic acid enzymes, made of DNA or RNA themselves, cut or join other nucleic acids. A docking-based switch keeps them off until their target is present. Understanding that design helps researchers build precise molecular tools, and it explains how cells avoid costly targeting mistakes.
plos-pone-0000773:
Ken Dawson-Scully, Gary A. B. Armstrong, Clement Kent and colleagues linked heat tolerance in nerves to one signaling enzyme, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Genetic variation is known to contribute to individual differences in thermotolerance, the ability to withstand heat. The specific genes and pathways involved, and how the environment modulates them, remained poorly understood. The team connects natural variation in neural function and behavior under heat to a cGMP-dependent protein kinase.

An enzyme best known from learning and feeding studies thus also helps set heat limits. As climates warm, the genes behind thermal tolerance move from academic to urgent. Model animals reveal which pathways might help or fail first.
plos-pone-0000873:
Thomas Hansen, Line Olsen, Morten Lindow and colleagues searched for brain microRNAs tied to schizophrenia, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Genes that code for proteins have long been the main target in schizophrenia genetics. MicroRNAs are short pieces of RNA that tune how genes are used, and they play a real part in brain growth and function.

That made microRNA genes fresh candidates for the search. The team focused on ones active in the brain and checked them for links to the illness. Work like this widens the hunt beyond protein genes alone. It also fits a view of schizophrenia as a disorder of how brain circuits are built and tuned.
plos-pone-0000973:
Kevin Langergraber, Heike Siedel, John Mitani and colleagues read the genetic signature of sex biased migration, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In many societies one sex leaves home to breed while the other stays. Patrilocal groups, where females move, include both chimpanzees and many human cultures.

The team compare DNA passed only through mothers with DNA passed only through fathers. Different migration by sex leaves opposite marks on those two records. Their study tests how clearly that signature shows in chimps and humans. A clear signature lets researchers read past social structure straight from present day genes.
plos-pone-0001073:
L. Niels Cornelisse, Ronald van Elburg, Rhiannon Meredith and colleagues filmed calcium surges in dendritic spines at high speed, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fast calcium changes in postsynaptic structures are crucial for synaptic plasticity, the tuning of connections that underlies learning. Most work had studied how calcium falls after a surge, not how it rises.

Using high speed two photon imaging, the team follow the rise in tiny dendritic spines. Rise speed sets how much calcium a spine's buffers must absorb, and how strong the signal becomes. Their work links the kinetics in a spine, a structure a micron wide, to the capacity of the whole synapse to change.
plos-pone-0001173:
Tuberculous meningitis, TB infection of the membranes around the brain, is a devastating condition that demands fast treatment. Maxine Caws and colleagues evaluated a diagnostic technique called MODS culture for the disease, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Rapid diagnosis remains elusive, since the standard smear test on spinal fluid misses most cases.

The MODS technique grows TB bacteria in liquid and watches for their distinctive growth under a microscope. The authors tested how well it identifies tuberculous meningitis. A faster, more sensitive test matters because every day of delay in starting chemotherapy raises the risk of death or lasting damage.
plos-pone-0001273:
Nerve cells release their chemical signals when an electrical signal opens calcium channels at the cell's ending. Roy Cohen, Merav Marom, and Daphne Atlas studied one protein in that release setup, syntaxin 1A, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Syntaxin works with the calcium channel and with other release proteins to couple excitation to secretion.

The authors report that depolarization-evoked secretion requires two neighboring cysteines in the part of syntaxin that spans the membrane, at positions 271 and 272. Two atoms' worth of chemistry decides whether secretion proceeds as it should. The finding pinpoints a vulnerable spot in the release mechanism.
plos-pone-0001373:
Carey Anders and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on breast cancer in young women. Breast tumors in women under age 45 tend to act more harshly than those in older women. The team wanted to learn what sets these young cases apart. They drew on records from 784 women with early stage disease.

From that group, 411 women met the study rules, split into a young group and an older group. The authors compared which cancer pathways were off track in each group. Their work maps how tumor biology shifts with age. Those maps may help doctors match care to the age and type of each case.
plos-pone-0001473:
Matthew Lohse and Alexander Johnson wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on two forms of a yeast that infects people. The yeast, Candida albicans, lives in the gut of most healthy people. It can switch at random between a white form and a dull opaque form. The team asked whether immune eater cells treat the two forms alike.

Using both fly and mouse eater cells, they found the forms are eaten at unlike rates. That gap may help the yeast hide or spread in the host. The work shows a shape shift can change how the immune system sees a germ. It adds a twist to how this common yeast causes grave ills.
plos-pone-0001573:
Jennifer Hayden and Sarah Ades published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a stress factor that keeps the E. coli cell skin sound. A class of backup gene switches sense stress in the cell's outer skin. One such switch is vital for the skin to hold in many germs. The team tested its role in the lab germ E. coli.

They show the factor is a must for keeping the cell skin intact in this germ too. Without it, the skin leaks and the cell fares poorly. Skin stress paths are drug targets, since our own cells lack them. Each firm fact here aids the hunt for new germ drugs.
plos-pone-0001673:
James P. Stewart, Anja Kipar, Helen Cox, and their co-authors studied airway responses to virus infection in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The focus is a family of messenger molecules called tachykinins. One of them, substance P, is a known driver of inflammation linked to nerve signals in the airways.

Earlier work on tachykinins in lung defense had centered on nerves. Stewart's team instead asked whether the airway lining itself, the epithelium, starts making tachykinins when a virus infects it. The full text gives the infection model, the molecule levels they measured, and where production rose. If the lining joins in, then airway inflammation has a local source that treatments for asthma and chest infections may need to address.
plos-pone-0001773:
Gerard A. J. Morris, Usman N. Ikumapayi, Martin Antonio, and their co-authors identified a new bacterial type from a sick baby in The Gambia, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Molecular diagnostic methods matter greatly in poor settings, where culture-based labs miss many infections and the true causes of illness stay murky.

A blood sample from a seven-month-old patient diagnosed with malaria in 2001 had grown nothing in culture. Molecular tests instead revealed a novel Campylobacter jejuni sequence type, a food-poisoning germ not previously recorded there. The full text gives the typing method and the sequence. One found case shows how much infection hides behind malaria diagnoses in West African clinics.
plos-pone-0001873:
Shiva Akbarzadeh and co-authors studied a cell-surface protein named ROR2 in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. ROR2 looks like a member of a known family of signal proteins, yet how it sends its signal was still unclear. The question counts because faults in ROR2 cause two human growth disorders, one of which shortens the fingers.

The team focused on one part of the protein, the part lost in the short-finger disorder, and tested what that part does. They report that the part is needed to switch ROR2 on, and that it works by drawing in a second protein, Src. That gives a concrete step in a pathway that shapes bone growth.
plos-pone-0001973:
Ruth Stavrum and co-authors compared the genomes of tuberculosis strains from Myanmar, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. One family of the TB bacterium, the Beijing family, dominates in East Asia and may spread or harm in unlike ways. Variety inside the TB genome may explain why strains differ in virulence.

No study of this kind had been done in Myanmar. The team set Beijing strains beside non-Beijing ones from the same country and charted their genomic diversity. A first map for a country fills a gap in the world picture of TB, and helps local labs track which strains drive their epidemic.
plos-pone-0002073:
Thimmaraju Rudrappa and co-authors studied poison-making bacteria around plant roots, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The rhizosphere, the thin soil zone around roots, is crowded: roots must cope with both harmful and helpful bacteria there. Some bacteria release their own chemical products that can steer root growth and the other microbe ties around them.

The team clarified the role of cyanide production by these pseudomonad bacteria. A poison made by one microbe can shape a whole web of interactions among plant, pathogen, and ally, a chain called multitrophic. Knowing the chain helps farmers use root bacteria to guard crops.
plos-pone-0002173:
Olivier Faivre and Mikko Juusola recorded how locust eyes turn light into signals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Photoreceptor cells capture the light that all later vision depends on, so their limits set the quality of everything the brain can see. The team placed fine electrodes in locust photoreceptors inside the living animal.

They showed the cells random flicker and natural-style patterns of light, then measured how faithfully the cells encoded each one. Comparing the two kinds of input shows how well the eye handles the scenes a locust actually meets in flight. Work like this links the physics of light to the design of an eye.
plos-pone-0002273:
Zhiyong Li, Yongzhu Yi, Xiangping Yin, and co-authors made foot-and-mouth disease vaccine proteins in silkworms, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Foot-and-mouth disease is a highly contagious illness of cattle, pigs, and other cloven-hoofed animals, and outbreaks cause severe farm losses. The traditional vaccine, made from killed virus, works, but making it carries a risk of accidental virus escape.

The team used a baculovirus system in silkworms to produce the virus's capsid proteins instead. Such subunit vaccines hold only pieces of the virus, so they cannot start an outbreak. The approach could make vaccination safer for the farms it is meant to protect.
plos-pone-0002373:
Gee, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Elaine P. S. Gee, Donald E. Ingber, Collin M. Stultz, among others. Its subject is fibronectin Unfolding Revisited: Modeling Cell Traction-Mediated Unfolding of the Tenth Type-III Repeat. Fibronectin polymerization is key for the development and repair of the extracellular matrix.

so, deciphering the mechanism of fibronectin fibril formation is of immense interest. The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002473:
Nosten-Bertrand and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Marika Nosten-Bertrand, Caroline Kappeler, Céline Dinocourt, among others. Its subject is epilepsy in Dcx Knockout Mice Associated with Discrete Lamination Defects and Enhanced Excitability in the Hippocampus. Patients with Doublecortin (DCX) mutations have severe cortical malformations linked to mental retardation and epilepsy.

Dcx knockout (KO) mice show no major isocortical abnormalities, but have discrete hippocampal defects. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002573:
Ngo and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Yen Ngo, Yves Benhamou, Vincent Thibault, among others. Its subject is an Accurate Definition of the Status of Inactive Hepatitis B Virus Carrier by a Combination. The rest of the title points to Biomarkers (FibroTest-ActiTest) and Viral Load. The combination of transaminases (ALT), biopsy, HBeAg and viral load have classically defined the inactive status of carriers of chronic hepatitis B.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002673:
In 2008, David Eriksson and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was Non-Linear population firing rates and voltage sensitive dye signals in visual areas 17 and 18 to short duration stimuli. The full author list in the catalog record begins with David Eriksson, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Visual stimuli of short duration seem to persist longer after the stimulus offset than stimuli of longer duration. A further point appears in the abstract. This visual persistence must have a physiological explanation. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002773:
In 2008, Karine Toupet and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about effective gene therapy in a mouse model of prion diseases. The catalog record names Karine Toupet first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Classical drug therapies against prion diseases have encountered serious difficulties. A further point appears in the abstract.
