It has become urgent to develop radically different therapeutic strategies. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002873:
Alison E. Coluccio, Rachael K. Rodriguez, Maurice J. Kernan and co-authors asked in 2008 whether yeast spores can live through a fruit fly gut. In nature, flies of the genus Drosophila eat yeast. When food runs short, the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae forms a dormant spore that resists heat and other stress.

Published in PLOS ONE, the study centers on the spore wall as the part that makes survival possible. It follows what happens when spores pass through the fly digestive tract. The work helps explain how yeast may spread from place to place by hitchhiking inside the flies that eat it.
plos-pone-0002973:
Shihui Yang, Quan Peng, Michael San Francisco and co-authors studied how plant chemicals switch on a bacterial secretion system in 2008. Dickeya dadantii infects a broad range of plant hosts. Its type III secretion system, a major virulence device, is governed by two main regulators.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team reports that phenolic acids from plants induce the system's genes. In other words, the pathogen senses plant chemistry and arms itself. Knowing the trigger helps plant pathologists think about blocking the signal before infection takes hold. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003073:
Manfred Gahr, Reinhold Metzdorf, Dieter Schmidl and co-authors measured the song nucleus HVC in a duetting songbird in 2008. Sex differences in brain area size are thought to link causally to sex differences in behavior and cognition. Which sex has the size advantage differs between areas and species.

In this species, pairs sing in unison, and both sexes sing. The team reports bi-directional sexual dimorphisms of HVC, meaning parts differ in opposite directions by sex. Published in PLOS ONE, unison song offers a rare check on simple male-larger stories of songbird brains. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003173:
Philly O'Riordan, Uli Schwab, Sarah Logan and colleagues report on fast drug resistance testing for tuberculosis in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Multi-drug resistant tuberculosis is a major public health concern because diagnosis is often delayed, raising spread to the community and health workers. Treatment is prolonged, and the total cost of a single case is high. Diagnosis had traditionally been slow.

Their case-control study tests whether rapid molecular detection of rifampicin resistance speeds early diagnosis and treatment of resistant disease. Readers get a practical check on a faster test where time matters. Quicker results can mean earlier correct therapy and less transmission.
plos-pone-0003273:
Jessica L. Dermody, Jonathan M. Dreyfuss, Judit Villén and colleagues study a yeast RNA-binding protein in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Production of a functional messenger RNA is regulated at every step of transcription. An area not well understood is the transition of RNA polymerase II from elongation to termination. The yeast SR-like protein Npl3 functions to negatively regulate transcription termination.

The title reports that unphosphorylated Npl3 stimulates RNA polymerase II elongation. Readers learn how one protein's phosphate state can switch its effect on the transcription machine. Such details explain how cells tune the length and amount of their messages.
plos-pone-0003373:
Daniel C. Richter and colleagues built a software tool called MetaSim, described here in 2008. Their field, metagenomics, reads DNA from whole habitats like soil or sea water. New sequencing machines were pouring out data faster than labs could check their methods. MetaSim makes fake sequencing data that acts like the real thing.

With fake data, scientists know the right answer before they start. They can test new analysis programs and see where the programs go wrong. The paper explains how the tool builds its test sets and what it can mimic. Such test data helps labs trust their results on real samples later.
plos-pone-0003473:
P. Christiaan Klink, Raymond van Ee, and Richard J. A. van Wezel tested old laws of vision in this 2008 paper. When each eye sees a unlike image, perception flips between them. Laws from Levelt describe how those flips behave. A second kind, perceptual rivalry, poses like puzzles.

It was unclear whether both kinds of rivalry share the same rules. The team found Levelt's propositions hold broadly across both. That shared behavior points to common computing steps in the brain. The work unites two classic windows onto conscious seeing. Rivalry tests are cheap and safe, which makes them a favorite probe of consciousness.
plos-pone-0003573:
Christian Mulder, Henri A. Den Hollander, and A. Jan Hendriks studied life in soil in this 2008 paper. Soil invertebrates reflect their habitat and most changes within it. They can serve as a universal currency for ecosystem quality. The team's goal was to find reference states for such living gauges.

Aboveground herbivory reshaped biomass distribution below ground. Grazing also altered the flux of soil invertebrates. Hungry mouths above thus quietly engineer the economy beneath. Soil checks must account for what happens on the surface. Soil life drives decay and soil carbon, both key to farm yields.
plos-pone-0003673:
Mikaël Lucas, Yann Guédon, Christian Jay-Allemand, and colleagues published this plant modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2008. A plant's root system takes shape mainly through branching, which lets it search patchy soil. The team modeled branching in Arabidopsis thaliana, a standard lab plant.

Their model runs on the transport of auxin, a growth hormone that flows through root tissues. It covers both steps of branch formation: where a side root starts and how it emerges. The math gives growers and biologists a way to predict root shape, a key part of how plants find water and food.
plos-pone-0003773:
Matthew R. Skerritt and Donald L. Campbell published this channel study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Potassium channels open and close in response to voltage, and a domain called S4 carries most of the charge that senses it. In Kv4 channels, one key position in S4 holds a neutral valine instead of a charged arginine.

The authors put a non-native arginine back at that R1 position in the Kv4.3 channel. The single swap uniquely altered how the channel gates. The change shows how precisely evolution tuned these electrical gates in different channel families.
plos-pone-0003873:
Matilde Marchi, Angela D'Antoni, Ivan Formentini, and co-authors compared two closely linked cell signals in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns ERK1 and ERK2, two kinases that carry signals into cells. Both respond to outside cues and help control growth, cell change, and memory links in the brain. Once switched on, both move into the cell nucleus.

The authors asked why two such alike kinases still act in distinct ways. They traced the split to the front end of ERK1, called its N-terminal domain. Swapping that part changed how the kinase behaved. The result shows how a small part of a protein can set its job apart.
plos-pone-0003973:
Frédéric Coutant, Marie-Pascale Frenkiel, Philippe Despres, and co-authors tested a safer viral vaccine carrier in 2008. Lentiviral vectors can start strong, lasting immune responses. That makes them attractive carriers for vaccines against tumors and tough germs. Safety worries have slowed their move into clinics.

Their PLOS ONE article uses a vector that does not integrate into cell DNA. Integration is the step feared to cause harm over time. The nonintegrative vaccine still conferred protective antiviral immunity in their tests. A safer carrier could widen use of this vaccine platform. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004073:
Mariantonietta Di Stefano, Maria Luisa Calabrò, Iole Maria Di Gangi, and co-authors tested herpesvirus infection of placenta in 2008. Placental herpes infection can harm pregnancy in several ways. It may cause growth problems, early delivery, or miscarriage. Human herpesvirus 8 had been linked to abortion and low birth weight.

Their PLOS ONE article studied HHV-8 infection in lab and pregnancy samples. Direct evidence in placental tissue tests those earlier links. Knowing whether the virus reaches the placenta guides screening debates. It also informs care for infected mothers in endemic regions. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004173:
Guillaume Mabilleau and Afsie Sabokbar published this bone study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Interleukin-32 is a recently described cytokine, a small immune signal made after stimulation by other signals such as IL-2, IL-18, and interferon gamma. It acts like a typical driver of inflammation, and a role in rheumatoid arthritis had recently been reported. IL-32 is one of the newer signals of its kind to be described.

The authors tested what IL-32 does to osteoclasts, the cells that break down bone. They report that it promotes the formation of new osteoclasts but does not switch on their bone-eating activity. That split matters for arthritis, where inflammation and bone loss do not always move together.
plos-pone-0004273:
Natalia Meani and colleagues published this zebrafish development study in PLOS ONE in 2009. PRDM genes form a family of transcriptional regulators that modulate cell differentiation, growth, and death. Some family members help tissues and organs mature, and they switch on and off at specific phases of embryonic development.

The team studied PRDM5, a family member known as a tumour suppressor. They report that PRDM5 regulates Wnt signalling at early stages of zebrafish development. Wnt is one of the master signalling systems of the embryo, so an early regulator of it shapes much that follows.
plos-pone-0004373:
When blood flow to the brain is cut off, as in a stroke, many cells in the cortex die. Thai Bui, Judith Sequeira, Tong Chun Wen, and co-authors published a 2009 PLOS ONE study on how some brain cells fight back. Their focus was a fast survival pathway switched on after cortical ischemia, the loss of blood flow to the cortex.

The authors report that a protein called ZEB1 links two related proteins, p63 and p73. That link forms a survival pathway inside neurons. The pathway switches on fast after injury. Work like this matters because stroke damage grows minute by minute. A built-in rescue route, once mapped, could point drug research toward helping cells hold on.
plos-pone-0004473:
Patterns where proteins grip small molecules are charted atom by atom by Ke Chen and Lukasz Kurgan in PLOS ONE in 2009. Shape fit and weak chemical forces are thought to drive how proteins bind small partner molecules, called ligands. Protein contacts with other proteins, DNA, and RNA had been studied in a systematic way, but contacts with small ligands had not.

The authors examined the atomic-level patterns in these binding sites across many known structures. They looked at which atoms meet, and what forces hold them together. A clear map of the rules helps computers predict where a drug molecule will sit on a protein. It also helps chemists design small molecules that grip their targets more firmly and cleanly.
plos-pone-0004573:
What people in Kisumu, Kenya believe about HIV treatment tracks with how common HIV is there, report Craig Cohen, Michele Montandon, Adam Carrico, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. When antiretroviral therapy became available in wealthy countries, unprotected sex and sexually transmitted infections rose, perhaps because fear of HIV fell. The team hypothesized a similar phenomenon might occur in sub-Saharan Africa.

They measured attitudes and beliefs toward antiretroviral therapy in the general population of Kisumu. They then set those attitudes beside HIV seroprevalence, the share of people testing positive. Linking beliefs to prevalence helps health programs judge whether treatment optimism is changing behavior. That knowledge shapes prevention campaigns in the treatment era.
plos-pone-0004673:
Byungchan Ahn and colleagues studied how the WRN protein unwinds DNA for a PLOS ONE paper in 2009. WRN belongs to a family of enzymes that help copy, repair, and protect DNA. It also helps care for the ends of chromosomes and fix some kinds of DNA damage.

The team showed that WRN can unwind DNA even when a small gap sits in the strand it moves along. Two partner proteins, POT1 and RPA, boost that action. The finding helps explain how cells keep copying past flaws. It also adds detail on a protein lost in a rare early aging illness.
plos-pone-0004773:
Dimitrios Koutsonanos and colleagues tested flu vaccination through the skin with vaccine coated microneedle arrays, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Flu causes outbreaks each year with thousands of hospital stays and deaths worldwide. Because the virus changes and immunity fades, vaccination is needed each year, yet coverage stays incomplete in many places.

Needle arrays offer a painless patch like route that could widen uptake. The team coated tiny needles with flu vaccine and applied them to skin. Skin delivery targets rich immune zones. If it works well, patches could simplify flu campaigns. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area.
plos-pone-0004873:
Aashir Awan, Aaron Bell, and Peter Satir showed Kin5 knockdown in Tetrahymena blocks cargo transport of Gef1 using RNA interference, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Intraflagellar transport builds and maintains the eukaryotic cilium. It utilizes kinesin superfamily members to transport cargo into the cilium and a dynein motor for retrograde traffic. A novel knockdown approach targeted the Kin5 kinesin in the ciliate model Tetrahymena thermophila.

Blocking anterograde transport strands specific cargo. Cilia defects underlie many human diseases called ciliopathies. Model ciliates allow fast genetic dissection. Gef1 delivery requires Kin5 specifically. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings.
plos-pone-0004973:
Muscle wasting follows bed rest, illness and starvation. A protein-shredding enzyme called Atrogin-1 drives much of that loss. Its substrates during wasting were poorly known. Julie Lagirand-Cantaloube and colleagues studied one target in PLOS ONE in 2009. The target is MyoD. MyoD controls muscle stem cell function and specialization.

Atrogin-1 tags MyoD for destruction by the proteasome. Blocking Atrogin-1 protected MyoD in living mice. With MyoD spared, skeletal muscle atrophy was prevented. The study flags the shredder as a drug target. Stopping it might protect patients whose muscles waste away during illness or immobility.
plos-pone-0005073:
Atherosclerosis is inflamed arteries slowly narrowing. Diet, blood pressure and blood lipids all feed it. Janet Chamberlain and colleagues studied one inflammatory driver in PLOS ONE in 2009. The driver is interleukin-1, an immune signal. They fed animals a fatty diet. Then they tracked several atherogenic mechanisms at once.

Interleukin-1 regulated multiple mechanisms in response to fat feeding. One signal coordinates much of the artery-clogging program. Blocking it could cool several pathways together. The finding ties diet, inflammation and vascular risk into one chain. It supports a focused treatment idea. Rather than chasing each mechanism separately, aim at their common conductor. The study gives that idea experimental weight.
plos-pone-0005173:
Limbs grow under the control of signal families that tell young cells where to form and what to become. Two proteins, Smad6 and Smad7, act as brakes on those signals. Vargesson and Laufer reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the chick versions of these brake genes.

The pair cloned one chick Smad6 gene and two forms of Smad7, then mapped where each is switched on in the growing limb. The maps show where growth signals are likely held in check during development. For biologists, the work fills in the control wiring that shapes arms, legs, and wings.
plos-pone-0005273:
Lupus is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own tissues. A peptide called P140, taken from a spliceosome protein, can calm lupus in mice. Page and colleagues explained how P140 works in PLOS ONE in 2009.

P140 is recognized by lupus T cells and briefly quiets their response to other targets. The team showed it interacts with the HSC70 protein and acts through a mechanism involving gamma-delta T cells. A defined mechanism strengthens the case for P140 as a lupus treatment. Lupus can harm the skin, joints, and kidneys at once, so a shot or pill form of this peptide could help many parts of the body with one line of attack.
plos-pone-0005373:
A human antibody called B7-DC XAb protects mice from tumors, both before and after tumors appear. It works by binding a molecule on dendritic cells, the immune system's sentries. Radhakrishnan and colleagues traced its downstream signaling in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Binding gathers a multi-protein cap on the dendritic cell and switches on signaling. The CD40 pathway is recruited indirectly, and T cell functions change as a result. Explaining the antibody's hidden wiring helps designers build better immune therapies against tumors. Tumors learn to hide from T cells, so a drug that wakes the sentry cells and. Through them, the T cells, takes a path that pure tumor poisons do not use at all.
plos-pone-0005473:
Takahito Kashiwagi and co-authors studied a flu virus enzyme part in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The flu virus copies its genome with an enzyme made of three parts. One part, called PA, helps the enzyme grip the start of a gene so copying can begin.

The team focused on the front end of PA from a bird flu strain found in Hong Kong. They tested how that end changes the enzyme's grip. Small differences there may help explain why some flu strains copy better in new hosts, a key step in how flu jumps between species.
plos-pone-0005573:
Iris Böselt and co-authors studied water saving in mammals in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Mammals live in habitats that range from lush to very dry. Along with kidney changes, hormone systems help them cope when water is scarce.

The team focused on the receptor for vasopressin in the kidney, which tells the body to hold on to water. They examined how that receptor is involved in adapting to a limited water supply. The work links one receptor to the wider story of how mammals colonised dry lands. Desert mammals push this system to its limits, and their versions of the receptor may hold extra lessons.
plos-pone-0005673:
Vijaya Musini and James Wright looked back at two large reviews of blood pressure trials in 2009, hunting for lessons the first reports missed. Their focus was blood pressure variability, the way readings swing up and down in one person. They asked how entry rules for a trial shape the numbers it reports.

The authors pose three plain questions about starting levels, swings, and trial design. Reviews built for one goal can still reveal facts about another, they argue. Their checks matter because doctors set drug doses from trial data. If entry rules skew the spread of readings, treatment advice built on them can mislead.
plos-pone-0005773:
Jean Lehmann, Michel Cibils, and Albert Libchaber explored in 2009 how a code could emerge as amino acids chained along RNA strands. The origin of the genetic code in an RNA world is a core puzzle of early life. Their setup lets amino acids polymerize on RNA templates and watches how the template steers the chain.

Both partners' traits shape the result: the RNA's sequence and the amino acids' chemistry. Order in the chains hints at how a code might start without any designer. Such lab models cannot replay history, but they can show which paths were possible. This one links chemistry to coding in plain steps.
plos-pone-0005873:
Branislava Janic and co-authors streamlined in 2009 a method for tagging cells with magnetic particles so they can be tracked by MRI. The standard FePro method mixes iron oxide with protamine and soaks cells overnight. That long process limits clinical and lab use.

The team optimized and validated a faster labeling protocol. Well-labeled cells can be followed after transplant to see where they go and how long they stay. That visibility is crucial for cell therapies, from stem cells to immune cells. A quicker, reliable label removes one bottleneck from imaging-guided treatment studies.
plos-pone-0005973:
A germ that lives in pigs can cause harsh meningitis in people who handle or eat pork. Heiman Wertheim, Huyen Nguyen, Walter Taylor and colleagues reported the scale of that risk in northern Vietnam in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper presents the first fifty cases of Streptococcus suis infection found there.

The germ is often missed, the authors note, because doctors do not expect it and tests can confuse it with other bacteria. A clear case series puts the disease on the map for clinics in the region. It also warns people who work with pigs, or who eat undercooked pork, that a rare germ can turn grave fast.
plos-pone-0006073:
A chemical colitis model is a workhorse of bowel disease research, yet its course is often loosely known. Yutao Yan, Vasantha Kolachala, Guillaume Dalmasso and colleagues charted that course in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper maps clinical signs and molecular changes over time and across gut regions in mice given dextran sodium sulfate, a compound that inflames the colon.

Bowel diseases like ulcerative colitis and Crohn's arise from genes and environment together, so a model's stages must be known to read drug tests fairly. A time-and-place map lets teams dose at the right stage and sample the right region. The work makes a common model more honest and more useful.
plos-pone-0006173:
Predators can shape the bodies of the animals they hunt, sometimes very fast. Fabrice Eroukhmanoff and Erik Svensson studied a small water isopod, a shrimp-like animal, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They looked at how defences against predators arose in parallel in separate groups, and how many traits changed together as one package.

Groups facing different hunters developed matching sets of defences over short spans of time. Body traits moved together rather than one by one, which the authors call integration of traits. The study shows that splits between groups can begin quickly when hunters differ. It gives students of evolution a neat case of change happening in the present day.
plos-pone-0006273:
Predicting whether a new protein will trigger allergies is a safety problem for food and medicine. Suchita Singh and colleagues tested whether whole-protein physical traits can forecast allergenicity in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Traits that change uptake by antigen presenting cells may tip a protein toward allergy.

The authors evaluate such properties as added predictors in computer screening. Catching likely allergens early saves costly lab work and protects trial volunteers. The approach complements sequence-based methods that miss physical behaviour. It is a step toward safer engineered proteins and novel foods.
plos-pone-0006373:
Orange pigments in roots store the raw material for vitamin A. Dirk Maass and colleagues raised levels of phytoene synthase in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. That enzyme starts carotenoid production, and the team raised it in Arabidopsis and carrot roots. The enzyme is a prime regulatory target, and boosting it had raised carotenoids in several crops.

Increased enzyme levels caused carotenoid crystals to form in the roots. Crystals show pigment packed beyond normal storage limits. Understanding that packing helps biofortification efforts for vitamin-poor diets. Carrot and the model plant Arabidopsis tell the same story here.
plos-pone-0006473:
Thorsten Schmidt, Hans-Werner Mewes, and Volker Stümpflen proposed a new signal for microRNA targets in PLOS ONE in 2009. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs that tune gene activity by binding target messages. Their target sites are very short, so binding alone looks unspecific. Recent experiments suggested extra context around the site shapes whether binding works.

The authors describe a putative enhancer signal that may strengthen target recognition. A better signal would improve computer predictions of which genes a microRNA controls. Prediction is a bottleneck in the field, since lab testing every candidate is slow. The proposal gives experimentalists a sharper place to look.
plos-pone-0006573:
Elise Nowbahari, Alexandra Scohier, Jean-Luc Durand, and colleagues documented rescue behavior in ants in PLOS ONE in 2009. Although helping behavior is ubiquitous throughout the animal kingdom, actual rescue activity is particularly rare. The team report the first experimental evidence of precise rescue in the ant Cataglyphis cursor. Ants freed entrapped relatives in their tests.

The rescuers directed their efforts precisely, digging and pulling where it mattered. Such targeted rescue goes beyond simple attraction to a nestmate in trouble. It suggests ants assess the situation and act accordingly. The study expands what social insects are known to do for each other.
plos-pone-0006673:
Dejia Li and colleagues tested a gene therapy idea in mice for PLOS ONE in 2009. Their target was oxidative stress, which is thought to weaken muscle contraction. Ordinary antioxidant supplements have failed to improve performance in tiring exercise. One problem may be that swallowed antioxidants never reach the right place inside muscle cells.

The team used an adeno-associated virus to place extra catalase inside mitochondria. Catalase is an enzyme that breaks down harmful oxygen compounds. Mice receiving the treatment were then tested for exercise performance. The approach asks whether protecting mitochondria directly can succeed where general antioxidants did not. It points toward more precise ways of protecting muscle during hard effort.
plos-pone-0006773:
Gregory S. Berns, Sara Moore, and C. Monica Capra scanned teen brains and asked about risky acts in PLOS ONE in 2009. The brain's white matter keeps growing through the teen years. It is not done until early adult life. That half-done state is often blamed for wild teen acts. The team tested that claim head-on in healthy teens.

Scans gauged how grown the white matter was in the front of the brain. Teens who did more risky acts had more grown white matter, not less. The result cuts against the simple blame-the-brain story. Taking risks rose as the front brain matured. The find forces a fresh look at why teens seek thrills.
plos-pone-0006873:
Jennifer Evertsen, Ramin Alemzadeh, and Xujing Wang tracked childhood type 1 diabetes in southeastern Wisconsin in PLOS ONE in 2009. Several studies confirm rising rates of the disease in children. Rising body weight at diagnosis has been linked to the trend. That link is called the accelerator hypothesis. Heavier children may stress insulin-producing cells faster.

The authors assessed whether regional incidence was truly changing. They related the change to body weight at diagnosis. Local data test whether national patterns hold in one community. If weight drives earlier onset, prevention gains a clearer target. The study adds a regional chapter to a global increase.
plos-pone-0006973:
Wei Wang, Wen Wang, Xiaopeng Mei, and colleagues studied nerve pain signals in the spinal cord in PLOS ONE in 2009. Nerve injury can leave lasting neuropathic pain. Both neurons and support cells called astrocytes in the spinal dorsal horn take part. How the two cell types talk to each other was not clear.

The team used rats with a tied spinal nerve, a standard pain model. They tracked signals passing between astrocytes and neurons after the injury. Mapping that crosstalk matters for treatment. Drugs that quiet the astrocyte side of the conversation might ease pain that painkillers barely touch.
plos-pone-0007073:
Bang-Ce Ye, Yan Zhang, Hui Yu, and colleagues recorded a bacterium's response to food signals in PLOS ONE in 2009. Microbes rebuild their gene activity to fit their surroundings. They sense the pools of nutrients inside themselves. The team used Bacillus subtilis, a well-studied soil bacterium.

A custom microarray covering more than four thousand genes tracked the response over time. The bacteria were fed three amino acids: valine, glutamate, and glutamine. Time-resolved profiles show which genes answer first and which follow. Such maps help engineers use this bacterium as a factory for useful products.
plos-pone-0007173:
Mayank Bhagat, Chitresh Bhushan, Goutam Saha, and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 on brain responses to colored flicker. Flickering light can trigger seizures in photosensitive epilepsy. Yet brain responses to different color combinations were still poorly studied when they began.

The authors record neuromagnetic signals while people see chromatic flickering stimuli. They analyze those signals with wavelet entropy, a math tool for measuring disorder in a signal over time. Their paper helps explain how the brain reacts to the colorful displays that surround daily life. It also offers a method other researchers can reuse for studying visual stimulation and seizure risk in the brain.
plos-pone-0007273:
Yixuan Gong, Evelyn Yao, Ronglai Shen, and colleagues tested a lung cancer drug target in PLOS ONE in 2009. The IGF-1 receptor pathway often goes wrong in human tumors. It had become an attractive target for anti-cancer therapy, including a fully human antibody called R1507.

The authors use a panel of non-small cell lung cancer cell lines. They ask which tumors are sensitive to the antibody in lab tests. They report that high total IGF-1 receptor levels track with sensitivity. Their biomarker work could help select patients most likely to benefit.
plos-pone-0007373:
Rosa H. Jimenez, Joan M. Boylan, Ju-Seog Lee, and colleagues compared drug responses in liver cell lines in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rapamycin blocks the mTOR pathway and shows anti-tumor activity in many cancers. Those cancers include hepatocellular carcinoma, the main form of liver cancer in adults worldwide today.

Resistance to rapamycin's growth-blocking effects is common, however. The authors hypothesize that tumorigenic and non-tumorigenic hepatic cell lines differ in response programs. They compare responsive and resistant lines to find shared patterns. Understanding resistance could guide combinations that make mTOR inhibitors work better in liver tumors.
plos-pone-0007473:
Amanda Spivak and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 using a seagrass habitat built as a controlled experiment. Ecosystems take in and release energy through producers, grazers, and decay. Both nutrient levels and food web makeup can shift that metabolism. Herbivores sit at the center of the web, moving plant material up the chain. The team varied both factors to see which mattered more.

Adding nutrients changed how the system produced and cycled energy. Changing the mix of plant-eating species changed it too, in its own way. The results show that who eats whom shapes an ecosystem as strongly as how much food is supplied. That matters for managing coastal habitats under pollution and fishing pressure. Simple nutrient rules alone will not predict how a seagrass bed behaves.
plos-pone-0007573:
Marion Guillaume and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 reading world records in sport as a record of politics. Earlier work used world records to probe the limits of human physiology. Political influence on sport had mostly been studied through Olympic medals. The team instead analyzed the full history of world records, nearly three thousand of them from dozens of nations. They sorted the marks by region and era.

Success in developing regions rose and fell with geopolitical change. Records track political history, not just bodies and training. Funding, stability, and state systems leave fingerprints on the stopwatch. That reframes the record book as a mirror of the twentieth century. It also warns against reading athletic limits as pure biology. The prism of politics changes what the same numbers mean.
plos-pone-0007673:
Eszter Deak, Selwyn Wilson, Elizabeth White and their co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the mold Aspergillus terreus. The mold makes a second kind of spore, called accessory conidia, beside its normal spores. The team compared the two spore types in close detail.

They found the accessory spores stand apart in three ways. Their outer surface has a distinct build, their walls are made of different material, and they sprout at a different pace. Those traits may help explain why this mold can thrive and, at times, cause disease in people.
plos-pone-0007773:
Alan Gillett and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It profiles gene activity in an animal model of multiple sclerosis. MS is a chronic disease that strips insulation from nerves and causes nerve loss. The model, called EAE, is widely used to study how MS develops.

Earlier work mostly tracked how much each gene is used. This team used genome-wide exon arrays instead. Those arrays can see alternative splicing, where one gene yields several message forms. Splicing changes may hide part of the disease process. The study opens that hidden layer to MS research.
plos-pone-0007873:
Sean Graham and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It maps how parasite-host networks are structured in nature. Ectoparasites, such as ticks and fleas, live on vertebrate hosts. Their networks show which parasite uses which host.

The authors tested whether those networks are nested. In a nested network, specialists use subsets of the hosts that generalists use. Consistent structure would help ecologists predict how vector-borne diseases spread. Lessons from well-studied networks could then transfer to new ones. The study provides one more piece of that structural map.
plos-pone-0007973:
Maya Bar and colleagues studied a brake on plant defense in PLOS ONE in 2009. Plants pull receptors in from their surface to start immune action, a step called endocytosis. A protein named EHD2 slows that pull-in for one tomato receptor, LeEix2.

The team showed the brake works through a coiled part of the protein. With that part in play, fewer receptors enter the cell and the defense signal fades. A brake may sound odd, but plants must keep defense from firing too hard; this work shows one way they hold it in check.
plos-pone-0008073:
Matthew Falagas and colleagues asked surgery patients in Athens how well their consent had been handled in PLOS ONE in 2009. Informed consent means a surgeon explains risks and choices before the knife, and the patient agrees with full knowledge. The study ran from late 2007 into 2008 across eight surgeons' patients.

Patients' grades showed gaps between the ideal and the bedside talk they recalled. Some felt rushed or under-informed about risks. Honest grades from patients themselves give hospitals a clear list of fixes, from plainer words to more time for questions.
plos-pone-0008173:
Vanesa Garcia and colleagues asked whether tumor messages floating in blood can foretell a lymphoma patient's fate in PLOS ONE in 2009. The cancer is diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Fragments of tumor RNA escape into the plasma, where a blood draw can reach them without a biopsy.

Levels of several such messages tracked with survival, some marking worse outlooks and others better ones. A panel of blood messages could thus sort patients by risk at low cost and low pain. That sorting could steer the strongest care to those who need it most.
plos-pone-0008273:
Lucas N. Joppa and Alexander Pfaff mapped protected areas worldwide in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. About an eighth of Earth's land surface lies in protected areas. Most were created during the twentieth century. Natural landscapes are critical for species survival. Protected areas also play a role in conservation and climate policy.

The authors found these areas are biased toward places that are high and far. Remote, steep land is easier to protect than fertile lowlands. That bias may leave many species and habitats exposed. Their analysis urges planners to protect land where nature needs it most.
plos-pone-0008373:
Wibeke Kinander, Torbjørn Bruvik, and Ulf R. Dahle typed tuberculosis strains in Norway in PLOS ONE in 2009. Norway had a high incidence of tuberculosis during the previous century. No molecular studies could be performed back then. Those epidemic strains have been disappearing over recent decades. Today, tuberculosis among native Norwegians is at the elimination stage.

The team identified dominant lineages in elderly patients born in Norway. Old strains surviving in older patients carry history in their DNA. Tracing them shows which epidemic families persist. It also helps separate reactivation from new importation.
plos-pone-0008473:
Aslam Ali Khan and co-authors study toxic shock in mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Toxic shock syndrome brings fever, rash, low blood pressure, and organ failure. It is caused by toxins from Staphylococcus aureus. One toxin is called SEB. SEB binds to immune cells and sets off a huge response. The team ask what role interleukin-2 plays in that response.

Interleukin-2, or IL-2, is a signal that grows T cells. In BALB/c mice, IL-2 regulates the shock that SEB induces. The results show how a single signal can scale the whole syndrome. That knowledge may help design ways to blunt toxic shock.
plos-pone-0008573:
Anthony Johnson and co-authors image rat brains during gut stimulation in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Visceral pain from the gut is the major complaint in irritable bowel syndrome. That syndrome, IBS, remains poorly understood. Brain imaging suggests defective brain-gut communication in IBS. Arousal centers in the brain appear overactivated in patients. The team use rats with amygdala implants of corticosterone, a stress hormone. They scan brains with fMRI during visceral stimulation.

Brain activation in these rats models the heightened arousal of IBS. The amygdala implants prime the brain to overrespond to gut signals. That model may reveal circuits to target for IBS pain. It connects chronic stress hormones to gut sensitivity.
plos-pone-0008673:
David Melzer, Neil E. Rice, Ceri Lewis, and co-authors published a public health study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It centers on bisphenol A, shortened to BPA, a chemical made in huge amounts for food and drink packaging. Traces of it show up in urine, which gives researchers a way to gauge exposure. Their data came from a national United States health survey.

Using survey records from 2003 to 2006, the team checked whether higher urine BPA lined up with heart disease. Earlier work on the same survey had raised similar questions about diabetes and liver enzymes. Their analysis again found heart disease more common at higher BPA levels. A urine link cannot prove cause, but it sharpened concern about routine exposure.
plos-pone-0008773:
Hiroaki Okuda, Ryusuke Kuwahara, Shinsuke Matsuzaki, and colleagues traced a schizophrenia-linked gene's reach in mouse brain. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene, Dtnbp1, makes a protein called dysbindin. It ranks among the top suspects for schizophrenia risk. What dysbindin controls inside brain cells was unclear. A fishing method that pairs proteins in yeast offered leads.

Dysbindin interacted with NF-YB, a gene-switch factor. Through it, dysbindin set the level of MARCKS, a signaling protein. A chain from risk gene to brain protein helps explain disease biology. Each link is a possible point for future treatment.
plos-pone-0008873:
Ugra Mohan Jha, Srinath Satyanarayana, Puneet Dewan, and colleagues profiled why tuberculosis patients in India quit treatment early. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. India's national program retreated many patients who had been treated before. More than fifteen percent of the 2006 group defaulted. Defaulting breeds drug resistance and continued spread. Knowing who defaults, and when, guides support efforts.

The team analyzed timing and traits of the defaulters. Certain groups and treatment phases carried higher risk. Programs can now aim reminders and support at those points. Reducing default is among the cheapest wins in TB control.
plos-pone-0008973:
Daniel Braun and co-authors studied how people learn the hidden pattern behind a movement task, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Learning is often pictured as slowly linking a sense signal to the right action. That picture treats learning as fitting a simple input-output map. But many tasks have structure, and learners may grasp the structure itself.

The paper models how a learner can discover that underlying structure. Instead of memorising each pairing, the learner guesses the rule that generates them. Once the rule is found, new situations can be handled without fresh training. The model speaks to both brain science and teaching machines to move.
plos-pone-0009073:
Thuy Do and co-authors fingerprinted 135 strains of the tooth-decay bacterium, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Streptococcus mutans is the mouth germ most tied to dental cavities. It tolerates acid well and drives tooth decay starting in childhood. The strains came from people with and without active caries, across several countries.

The team used MLST, a typing method that reads several housekeeping genes. Comparing the fingerprints showed how much diversity the species holds overall. Strains also shuffled their genes, generating fresh combinations over time. A diversity map helps explain why decay risk differs from mouth to mouth.
plos-pone-0009173:
Branislava Janic and co-authors grew cord blood progenitor cells for a long stretch and checked their identity, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Progenitor cells for vessel lining can help rebuild damaged blood vessels. That promise makes them candidates for treating diseases of poor circulation. Cord blood offers a young and rich source of such progenitor cells.

The cells under study carry a surface marker called AC133. After long growth in culture, they kept their vessel-progenitor traits intact. Cells that survive mass growth without losing character are the ones therapy needs. Growing enough cells, without drift, is the bottleneck for cord blood treatments.
plos-pone-0009273:
Yoko Kubo and co-authors published this frog study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cryptochromes are proteins related to light-repair enzymes called photolyases. In some animals they help run the daily clock or sense blue light. Others may even help animals sense magnetic fields.

The team measured where cryptochrome genes are active in the African clawed frog, Xenopus tropicalis. The genes turned out to be highly expressed in the ovary. Strong activity in eggs and ovaries hints at a role beyond the usual clock story. The finding opens a new place to look for what these versatile proteins do.
plos-pone-0009373:
Umar Farooq and co-authors published this injury study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Violence and deliberate self-harm send many people to hospitals in Pakistan. How many cases reach the police, versus only the hospital, was unclear. The setting was Rawalpindi, a city of about 1.6 million people.

The team compared injuries reported to health authorities with those reported to police. The two records captured different slices of the same problem. Gaps between them mean official crime figures understate real violence and self-harm. Knowing the gap helps planners size services for victims who never enter police files.
plos-pone-0009473:
Ekaterina Litvinova and colleagues reported a surprising link between scent and flu in mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. A female mouse ready to mate gives off a scent signal. Males that smell it start to search for a mate. That search brings close contact with scent marks, which could carry germs. The team exposed males to the scent and then tested their response to flu.

Males that had smelled the female scent resisted influenza better than other males. The gain came even though close sniffing should raise exposure to germs. The study ties a mating signal to a stronger defense against infection. It shows that social cues can tune the immune system in unexpected ways.
plos-pone-0009573:
Simon Greenhill, Alexei Drummond, and Russell Gray tested language family trees in PLOS ONE in 2010. Austronesian languages spread across the Pacific with seafaring peoples. One account says they began in Taiwan about five thousand years ago and moved in pulses with pauses. The team had earlier used computer methods on word data to build trees for these languages. Now they asked how accurate and robust those trees are.

They checked the trees against other data and methods. Sound trees should stand up to such stress tests. The work backs the pulse and pause account of Pacific settlement. It also shows how language data can test stories of human migration across the largest ocean on Earth.
plos-pone-0009673:
Bernice Wright and co-authors traced a food compound through blood platelets in PLOS ONE in 2010. Quercetin is a flavonoid found in onions, apples, and many plants. It is praised for possible health effects. What reaches the body's tissues, though, may differ from what is swallowed. The team studied how platelets, the blood's clotting cells, change quercetin.

Platelets metabolized the compound, producing altered forms of it. So the blood itself edits a dietary molecule before tissues see it. That editing could raise or lower the compound's effects. Any claim about quercetin's benefits must reckon with the forms that actually circulate.
plos-pone-0009873:
Health anxiety makes people fear serious illness despite reassuring tests. Per Fink, Eva Ørnbøl, and Kaj Sparle Christensen followed such patients in primary care for two years. Their follow-up study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Primary care is the first-stop medicine of family doctors and clinics. The team tracked two outcomes: health care costs and self-rated health. Persistent anxiety can drive repeated visits and tests, raising costs without easing fear. Knowing the two-year course helps doctors plan steadier care for these patients. Costs were counted in money, health in patients' own ratings.
plos-pone-0009973:
Herpes simplex virus type 2 causes genital herpes that can flare again and again. Bulbulgul Aumakhan and colleagues studied people carrying both HSV-2 and HIV. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Clinical reactivations are the visible flare-ups of the herpes infection. The team compared those flares with markers of HIV disease progression. Markers include virus levels and immune cell counts in blood. Two chronic viruses in one body can push each other along. Knowing the link helps doctors manage patients who carry both. Both viruses stay in the body for life once caught.
plos-pone-0010073:
Tamara Romanuk and Colin Levings studied a shoreline food web in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Their site was a temperate zone where land meets the sea. They used stable isotope analysis, a chemical fingerprint method, to trace carbon sources. Invertebrates there were sampled from low shore up to land above the tide line.

The question was how much food energy crosses between land and sea, in both directions. Those flows, called reciprocal subsidies, lead along food web pathways to young chum salmon. The work shows salmon fry depend on a wider landscape than the water alone.
plos-pone-0010173:
The authors were Barbara Tillmann, Pierre Jolicœur, Masami Ishihara, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tested people born unable to process music normally. The condition, congenital amusia, was usually blamed on poor pitch processing. A recent claim instead blamed a general spatial processing deficit, which would recast the disorder entirely.

The team assessed spatial abilities in amusic people alongside their music skills. Their title sums up the outcome: these listeners are lost in music, but not in space. That result defends the pitch account and narrows where researchers should look in the brain.
plos-pone-0010273:
The authors were Satoshi Yamaji, Jun Saegusa, Katsuaki Ieguchi, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study engineered a growth factor that blocks its own family. FGF proteins signal through receptors and through integrins, cell anchors, with crosstalk between them. The team had found that FGF1 binds an integrin directly, at a site distinct from its receptor binding site.

From that split, they built an FGF1 mutant that acts as an antagonist, a blocker. A blocker shaped from the factor itself could halt growth signals in cancer or excess blood vessel growth. The mutant also serves as a tool to separate signaling routes.
plos-pone-0010373:
Jürgen Glas and colleagues tested a gene called STAT4 across several immune diseases in PLOS ONE in 2010. Variants of STAT4 had already been linked to lupus and rheumatoid arthritis. That pattern hints that different autoimmune diseases share some root genes. The team asked whether the same gene also raised risk for Crohn's disease, a gut inflammation. They focused on one common variant in the gene.

That variant was tied to Crohn's affecting the colon, and to earlier onset of disease. A shared gene across lupus, arthritis, and gut disease suggests shared immune pathways. Shared pathways could mean shared treatments one day. The study adds Crohn's to the list of conditions in STAT4's reach. Genetics, here, redraws the borders between diseases.
plos-pone-0010473:
Thomas Couvreur and colleagues tested how starting assumptions sway family-tree studies of plant form in PLOS ONE in 2010. A popular method rebuilds ancestral traits on evolutionary trees using Bayesian statistics. Like all Bayesian work, it needs prior values set in advance. Those priors can quietly steer the answers. The team used the custard apple family, Annonaceae, as a case study in plant shape traits.

They varied the priors and watched how trait histories changed. If conclusions swing with assumptions, researchers must report that honestly. Morphology on trees informs how flowers and fruits evolved. The study is a caution and a guide for that whole method. Good priors, it argues, are part of good evidence.
plos-pone-0010573:
Fan Xiu Zhu, Narayanan Sathish, and Yan Yuan reported a virus study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was a herpesvirus linked to Kaposi's sarcoma, a cancer seen most often in people with weak immune systems. The team focused on one viral protein, called ORF45, packed inside each virus particle.

Infected cells normally raise an alarm that slows virus growth. The experiments show ORF45 helps the virus muffle that alarm. By blocking early warning signals, the protein lets the virus copy itself more freely. Knowing how this blocking works could guide drugs aimed at viruses that hide from immune defenses.
plos-pone-0010673:
Panagiotis Papatheodorou and colleagues traced how clostridial toxins enter cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Clostridium difficile toxins A and B cause severe gut illness, often after antibiotic treatment. Related toxins come from other clostridia. All of them add a sugar tag to proteins inside the cell, which wrecks cell shape.

The team watched the toxins at the cell surface and just inside it. The toxins entered through pits coated with a protein called clathrin. Blocking that route slowed toxin entry. A shared doorway is good news for drug design, since one blocker might blunt several toxins at once.
plos-pone-0010773:
Mathieu Brodeur and colleagues released a shared set of object photos for mind research, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Experiments on language and vision need pictures whose traits are already measured. Without shared norms, each lab picks its own pictures and results cannot be compared fairly.

The Bank of Standardized Stimuli holds 480 photos of everyday objects. Volunteers rated each photo for familiarity, name agreement, and visual complexity, among other traits. Any lab can now run studies on the same pictures with the same ratings. Shared tools like this quietly raise the quality of hundreds of later experiments.
plos-pone-0010873:
J Tiago Gonçalves and Walter Stühmer published this biophysics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ion channels act as gates for electric signals in cells, and the potassium channel EAG1 is shut down by calcium acting through a sensor protein called calmodulin. Three possible grip sites on the channel had been proposed, but which ones matter in the real channel was unsettled.

The authors tagged the channel and the sensor with glowing labels and watched them interact inside living mammalian cells using a light-based proximity method. Two sites did most of the work: a high-affinity site near one end of the channel and one near the other end. Mutating those sites wiped out binding. Gonçalves and Stühmer settle how a calcium signal grabs this channel, a step toward understanding its roles in nerve and muscle activity.
plos-pone-0010973:
John Harp and Thandi Onami published this T cell trafficking study in PLOS ONE in 2010. For T cells to leave the blood and enter tissues, they first tether to vessel walls using sugar tags called selectin ligands, built by enzymes including two fucosyltransferases. The authors studied mice lacking both enzymes to see how lung traffic changes when the tethers are missing.

Unexpectedly, naive T cells piled up in the resting lung tissue of these mice, at about five times normal numbers, without any inflammation. After viral infection, though, activated T cells were reduced in the inflamed lung, matching the known entry role of the tags. Harp and Onami reveal a split picture: the same missing tether can overfill a quiet organ and starve an inflamed one. That nuance matters for drugs that block cell migration.
plos-pone-0011073:
Jason Kamilar and Kathleen Muldoon published this primate evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A classic prediction says close relatives should live in similar environments, while adaptive radiations, where one lineage explodes into many niches, may break that rule. Madagascar's lemurs are a textbook radiation, and the authors gave them the first test of ecological diversity in a family-tree framework.

They assembled occurrence records for more than forty living species, matched each locality with climate data, and summarized every species' climatic niche along rainfall and temperature axes. Statistical tests then asked whether niche similarity fades with evolutionary distance as the classic prediction demands. Kamilar and Muldoon use an island radiation to probe how fast ecology can decouple from ancestry, a question central to explaining Madagascar's extraordinary primate variety.
plos-pone-0011173:
Osenberg, Paz Yaacov, Safran and colleagues measured RNA editing in PLOS ONE in 2010. Human embryonic stem cells copy certain repeated DNA regions into RNA. An enzyme family then edits those copies by swapping one RNA letter for another, a process the team measured in cells not yet specialized.

Editing levels in these repeated regions were high in the unspecialized stem cells. Heavy editing may help fine tune which genes the young cells express. It also marks stem cells as a special state for RNA control. Understanding that state matters for using stem cells safely in research and medicine.
plos-pone-0011273:
Bjork, Welling, Laakso and colleagues measured open access in PLOS ONE in 2010. By 2009, a growing share of research papers could be read free online, but how large that share was remained disputed. The team surveyed the state of free access to the scientific journal literature that year.

Their snapshot maps how far the open movement had come and where barriers remained. Funders and universities use such numbers to push publishing reform. Free reading matters most for doctors, teachers and researchers without rich library budgets. The 2009 baseline lets later studies judge how fast science is opening up.
plos-pone-0011373:
Matthew Brown and co-authors reported in 2010 a simpler source for making stem cells from a person's own body. Induced pluripotent stem cells can become many cell types, but they were usually made from skin, which needs a biopsy. The team instead started with T lymphocytes, the immune cells that a routine blood draw already provides in large numbers.

They reprogrammed those blood cells back into a stem-cell state able to form varied cell types. A blood-based route removes a painful step and uses samples clinics already collect and store. That ease matters for building patient-specific cells for research and, in time, therapy. The paper helped move stem cell work toward sources that patients can give with little burden and labs can obtain on demand.
plos-pone-0011473:
Katie Slocombe, Tanja Kaller, and Josep Call showed in 2010 that chimpanzees read social news in the screams of others. During fights, chimpanzees scream, and bystanders who only hear the fight still learn from it. The team played recorded screams from past conflicts to captive chimpanzees and watched how the listeners responded to the animals involved.

Listeners behaved as if they knew who had fought whom and how the fight had gone, adjusting their own behavior toward the participants. Screams thus carry information about third-party conflicts, not just distress. Eavesdropping of this kind lets a chimp track shifting alliances without witnessing every fight. For the study of social intelligence, the work shows our closest relatives gather social knowledge much as humans do, by listening in.
plos-pone-0011573:
Fredros Okumu, Nicodem Govella, and Sarah Moore weighed in 2010 a promising malaria tool: traps baited with human odor. Mosquitoes find people by smell, so a trap that smells like a person could lure malaria vectors away from sleepers and kill them. The team assessed the potential benefits and limitations of such traps for malaria control in Africa and sketched target product profiles, the specifications a winning device must meet.

Their analysis tells designers what a trap must do, in catch rates, durability, cost, and power needs, and what could sink it, from competing real hosts to maintenance in remote villages. A profile written before mass production saves the field from elegant traps that fail in the field. Odor-baited traps will not replace nets and spraying soon, but a clear-eyed specification is how a promising idea becomes a shippable product.
plos-pone-0011673:
Francis Béby and co-authors removed a developmental gene from the adult mouse eye, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Otx2 is essential for building the forebrain and head before birth, and it stays strongly active in the adult retina. Human mutations in this gene cause eye defects, hinting at a continuing maintenance role.

Deleting Otx2 only in adulthood triggered fast decay of the retinal pigment layer and slow loss of light-sensing cells. The two-speed decline shows what fails first when this regulator disappears. The work helps explain inherited retinal disease and what adult eyes still owe to a childhood gene.
plos-pone-0011773:
Brendon King and co-authors studied sunlight's effect on a waterborne parasite, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ozone loss, warming and souring waters have raised the sun's rays reaching many lakes and seas, with growing harm to water life. Cryptosporidium parvum is a tough parasite that causes gut disease through tainted water.

The team found sun rays cause damage outside the parasite's nucleus and set off a false start in its timed release process. A parasite tricked into firing its entry tools early may fail to infect. That finding points to weak spots in a germ famed for resisting treatment.
plos-pone-0011873:
Rabindra Bhattacharjee and colleagues traced in 2010 how worn chromosome ends can set off deadly inflammation in mice. Telomeres cap chromosomes and keep them stable, but they shorten with age and division. The team used mice lacking a telomere-maintaining RNA part, whose cells show high chromosome instability.

In these mice, unstable chromosomes triggered inflammation through TLR4, an immune alarm receptor, and the reaction could end in death. The chain links a basic sign of aging, short telomeres, to immune harm across the whole body. It raises the possibility that some damage blamed on old age runs through this alarm pathway and might be softened there.
plos-pone-0011973:
Yong Suk Hur and colleagues presented in 2010 evidence for a new signaling setup inside astrocytes, the brain's support cells. Astrocytes release messenger chemicals, called gliotransmitters, that let them talk to neurons. These messengers, including glutamate and ATP, are stored in vesicles and released on signal.

The evidence points to a system based in secretory granules, also called dense-core vesicles, that uses the calcium signal IP3 to control release. A second storage and release route changes the picture of how astrocytes join brain conversations. Since astrocyte signaling shapes synapses and blood flow, its machinery is a growing target in brain research.
plos-pone-0012073:
Fabio Richlan and co-workers asked in 2010 whether two very different reading problems share one brain fault. Developmental dyslexia in German-speaking readers shows up as slow, effortful reading with accuracy mostly intact. Stroke patients with letter-by-letter reading share that slow pattern, gained in adulthood after brain injury.

Using fMRI, the team found both groups showing abnormal effects in the same left occipito-temporal region, the area that normally recognizes written words at a glance. A common dysfunction would unite a childhood condition and an acquired one under a single mechanism. That gives dyslexia research a lesion model to learn from, and rehabilitation a shared target.
plos-pone-0012173:
Naval Shanware, Lihong Zhan, John Hutchinson, and co-authors studied how a family of gene switches is controlled, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The CREB and ATF1 switches help cells respond to signals and stress, turning gene programs on at the right moments. A cleanup enzyme complex can dial these switches down, and DNA damage adds its own layer of control on top.

The team compared how the enzyme complex handles each family member, under calm conditions and under DNA-damaging stress. Some control routes are shared and some are private to one switch. These details matter because the same switches are misused in cancers and in diseases of memory and metabolism, where restoring normal control is the goal.
plos-pone-0012273:
Kelli Ryckman, Katherine Fielding, Adrian Hill, and co-authors examined how inherited variants shape response to the hepatitis B vaccine, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The vaccine prevents a major world health burden, yet people respond unevenly, and some barely respond at all. The team had earlier tied single-letter DNA variants in several candidate genes to the height of the antibody peak after vaccination.

Here they analyzed combinations of variants inherited together, which can reveal effects single variants hide. Knowing which genetic patterns predict weak response could let clinics give extra doses to exactly the people who need them. It is a step toward vaccination schedules fitted to the person, not just the calendar.
plos-pone-0012373:
Masamitsu Negishi, Atsunori Saraya, Shinobu Mochizuki and co-workers identified a new player in gene silencing in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. A gene locus called Ink4a/Arf guards against cancer, and Polycomb protein groups keep it switched off in young cells. When the guard is silenced at the wrong time, cancer risk rises, yet how Polycomb finds this locus was unclear.

The team found that a zinc finger protein, Zfp277, helps Polycomb complex 1 settle on the locus and repress it. The discovery fills a gap in how cells lock down a key tumor guard. It also gives cancer researchers a new handle on the aging and growth controls tied to this famous locus.
plos-pone-0012473:
Mayu Inaba, Hebao Yuan, Viktoria Salzmann and colleagues studied stem cells that make sperm in fruit flies, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. These stem cells sit in a niche, a pocket that tells them to stay stem cells. To divide the right way, a stem cell must aim its spindle so one daughter stays in the niche and the other leaves to mature.

The team showed that the adhesion protein E-cadherin is required to orient the centrosomes and spindle correctly. Without it, divisions go awry and stem cell balance breaks. The same adhesion-based aiming appears in many stem cell niches, so the fly work speaks to human tissue maintenance too.
plos-pone-0012573:
Mark van Eekelen, John Overvoorde, Carina van Rooijen and colleagues cataloged an enzyme family in zebrafish, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Protein-tyrosine phosphatases remove phosphate tags and, working against kinases, govern cell survival, growth, movement, and specialization. The classical family members had not been fully listed for the zebrafish, a workhorse of developmental genetics.

The team identified and mapped expression of the full classical phosphatase family in zebrafish. A complete roster lets geneticists pick the right members to knock out and watch development fail or adapt. Zebrafish findings translate unusually well to human biology, so the catalog serves disease research too.
plos-pone-0012673:
Fernandez-Rozadilla, de Castro, Clofent and co-authors tested gene variants in two growth pathways for bowel cancer risk. Bowel cancer arises from many small genetic and life factors rather than one strong gene. Their 2010 study worked with a Spanish patient group, reading single-letter DNA changes in the Wnt and BMP pathways.

Both pathways guide gut cell growth, so faults in them are natural suspects. Sorting which variants truly raise risk helps build screening tools for families. It also sharpens the picture of how this common cancer begins.  The cohort design keeps ancestry and setting fairly uniform.
plos-pone-0012773:
Caballero, Zhao, Rimoldi and co-authors found frequent mutations in the MAGE gene family in human melanoma. MAGE genes belong to a group normally active only in the germ line and in some tumours. Because of that pattern, their products are favourite targets for cancer vaccines and immune treatments.

Their 2010 survey of melanoma samples found these genes mutated surprisingly often. Mutations can change how the immune system sees a tumour, for better or worse. The finding tells vaccine designers to check each patient's MAGE status before aiming at those targets.
plos-pone-0012873:
Jaoko, Karita, Kayitenkore and co-authors ran an early safety trial in Africa of a two-step HIV vaccine plan. Their 2010 study was a double-blind trial with placebo control, the strictest kind of early test. Volunteers received a recombinant adenovirus vaccine carrying HIV Gag and Pol genes, alone or after a DNA vaccine prime.

The team measured safety and how strongly immune systems answered. Early trials like this one decide whether a vaccine idea earns larger tests. Running them in Africa also ensures the data fit the populations most affected by HIV.
plos-pone-0324673:
Eric W. Lee and co-workers compare computer models that flag children at risk of anxiety disorders from their medical records. Early warning could help clinics step in before anxiety takes hold. Their 2026 study trains several standard learning models and several deep learning models on structured health records, with and without added neighborhood-level health measures for each child's area.

Models that read a child's record history over time performed best overall. A strong standard model using recent record snapshots also did well and was simpler to run. Adding neighborhood measures brought little gain in either case. The work shows routine records already carry useful warning signs, which could support earlier, kinder outreach to families.
plos-pone-0337873:
Aninda Astuti and four colleagues break cancer networks into small regulatory teams to find the ones driving metastasis. Their 2026 study builds a bioinformatics framework around gene regulatory modules: tiny groups of genes acting together. Modules were extracted from molecular networks and ranked by a combinatorial fusion method. Kidney cancer metastasis cohorts supplied the test beds. The top-ranked modules were cross-examined against cancer hallmark lists, drug-target databases, and patient survival data.

The framework beat existing methods at flagging metastasis-linked modules. Its choices stayed stable across ten different feature combinations. Three-gene and four-gene module versions performed consistently as well. Spread, not the primary tumour, is what usually kills cancer patients. Modules that reliably mark spread could nominate both warning biomarkers and drug targets. Because the method reads coordination rather than single genes, it may catch drivers that one-gene-at-a-time hunts keep missing.
plos-pone-0338173:
Andrea Anton and four colleagues sound the alarm over an invading green alga spreading through a Spanish lagoon, in this 2026 PLOS ONE survey study. First spotted in 2020 in Estany des Peix on Formentera, the alga Batophora occidentalis had reached every surveyed spot in the lagoon by 2023. The team measured its cover and weight across the seagrass and algae meadows that shelter local marine life.

In two native meadows it became the most abundant plant-like organism present. It also grew over the leaves of protected Neptune grass, at times weighing several times the leaf itself, and fouled a fifth of the boats in the marina. One specimen outside the lagoon suggests escape has begun — the authors urge containment now.
plos-pone-0340173:
Anneke de Weerd and seven colleagues publish a protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026 for following teenagers through a specialised therapy for borderline personality traits, in the Netherlands. The therapy works for many adolescents but not all, and nobody knows exactly which changeable ingredients — trust in the therapist, emotional weather between sessions, motivation — make the difference. Fifteen young people at four treatment centres will be followed for nine months.

The adolescent, their parents, and their therapist will each be interviewed four times along the way, producing one hundred and eighty conversations. Comparing the three viewpoints as they shift should reveal where therapy gains or loses traction, giving therapists concrete levers to pull when a case stalls.
plos-pone-0342273:
Godlove Chaula and five colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One laboratory study on improving the oldest tuberculosis test still in wide use, the stained sputum smear. Its weakness is losing bacteria during sample preparation. The team tried spinning samples harder and longer during the concentration step, using both lab-grown bacteria and real patient sputum, then graded the resulting smears.

Spinning harder did not turn more smears positive, in either sample type. It did make positive clinical samples grade higher, meaning more bacteria visible per field, and a longer spin at standard force had the same effect on real sputum. The authors say tuning this cheap preparation step can make smear results more informative for tracking treatment, even if it does not catch additional cases.
plos-pone-0343973:
Shubbham Gupta, Isobel Claire Gormley, and Lorraine Brennan introduce a software method for spotting when one person's metabolism drifts away from its own normal pattern. Blood metabolites shift with genes, food, and lifestyle, and a change inside one person can warn of illness earlier than a single odd reading. Their model, MetaboVariation 2.0, judges all measured metabolites together rather than one at a time.

Considering metabolites jointly matters because these chemicals rise and fall together. In simulated data the combined model beat the earlier one-at-a-time version, especially when metabolites moved in step. Applied to repeated blood samples from one hundred and sixty-four people, it flagged about one person in seven as showing an unusual internal shift at some visit. The authors offer it for studies tracking health over time.
plos-pone-0346073:
Nurnazira Hanis Mustaffar Kamal and co-authors searched in 2026, by computer, for flavonoids from natural products that might fight hyperlipidaemia, the excess of fats in the blood that raises heart disease risk. Flavonoids are plant chemicals found in many foods and traditional remedies. The team used computational approaches to screen them against targets involved in handling blood fats.

Screening in the computer first lets researchers test far more compounds than a laboratory could, and discard the unlikely ones early. The candidates that survive still need bench testing before anyone can call them treatments. The study reflects a standard modern route to drug discovery, in which traditional plant knowledge and molecular modeling narrow the search together.
plos-pone-0346673:
Mohamed Musa and co-workers build a defense against flood-style cyberattacks on modern wide-area business networks. These networks route traffic by software, which adds flexibility but also gives attackers a central target to overwhelm. Their 2026 paper trains learning models on attack data gathered in controlled tests, aiming to spot both heavy floods and quieter, low-rate ones.

The combined model sorted high-rate and low-rate attacks with very high accuracy in testing. A data-shrinking step kept accuracy while cutting the work involved. The system also reacts on its own when attack traffic first appears, rather than waiting for human action. The authors note that live-network trials still need to confirm how well the defense holds up outside the lab.
plos-pone-0346973:
Rachel Berns and colleagues compared injury troubles between young runners and master runners over thirty-five. Two hundred seven runners completed an online survey about training habits and injuries that limited their running. Older runners are often assumed to cope worse, but detailed comparisons by age are scarce, and the 2026 study aimed to fill that gap.

Master runners reported more limitation: about half had been held back by injury, against a third of younger runners, and they suffered more arm and shoulder problems. Smoking, gravel surfaces, and even owning many shoes were linked to their troubles. Younger runners fared better with coaches, varied surfaces, and off-road tracks. The authors call for age-specific prevention advice.
plos-pone-0347073:
Da-Bin Lee led a team of seven authors building a fast air quality model for South Korea, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Full chemistry models like CMAQ predict how emission cuts change ozone and fine particles, but they run slowly on supercomputers. The team built a reduced-form version using a method called LASSO to keep only what matters most.

Lee's surrogate model lets policymakers test clean-air scenarios in minutes instead of days. Fast answers change what is possible in a policy debate: options can be compared live, not one per week. The trade-off is some precision, which the team must keep honest. For a country wrestling with seasonal smog, a fast and faithful model is a practical public health tool.
plos-pone-0347473:
Kim Lara Lühmann and colleagues catalog a strange kind of RNA in crop sap. Their plant study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The crop is oilseed rape. Its sap stream, the phloem, carries signals around the plant. The cargo includes circular RNA, loops that resist decay. Such loops could travel far and still work.

The team sequenced the sap and found more than seventeen hundred distinct loops. They confirmed a sample with lab tests. Full-length reads covered loops from sap and from leaves. A few strong candidates for signal roles stood out. Oilseed rape is a major world crop. Knowing what rides in its sap may help breeders track stress.
plos-pone-0347873:
Khanh Giang Le builds a crash prediction system that puts safety ahead of raw accuracy, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper using United Kingdom accident data from 2020 to 2024. Most models chase overall correctness, which can mean missing the rare crashes that kill or seriously injure, exactly the ones road policy cares about.

His model splits crashes into two classes: slight injuries in one, deaths and grave injuries in the other. It corrects the imbalance between the classes, tunes its decision line for safety, and calibrates its odds so the stated risk can be trusted. Explanation tools then show which factors drive each prediction. A model that admits its reasoning is easier for road authorities to act on than a more accurate black box.
plos-pone-0348073:
Parya Jangipour Afshar and co-workers review what happens when clinics merge services for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and other sexually transmitted infections into one program. These infections overlap in risk and testing, so joined care could save trips and money. Their 2026 review gathers one hundred eighteen studies and reports from thousands of initial hits across world literature.

Merged programs improved health results, cut costs, prevented spread, and raised patient knowledge in many settings. They also strained staff, budgets, and buildings when support lagged. Benefits clustered around shared delivery, shared records, and partnerships. The authors conclude integration pays when health systems fund the extra load it creates, rather than simply declaring services joined.
plos-pone-0348173:
Gyu-Seong Lee and colleagues tackle two linked questions in early drug development in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper: how fast the body clears a drug, and how widely it spreads through tissues. Both properties decide dosing, and they influence each other, yet most prediction tools treat them separately and use only one kind of molecular description.

Their multi-task boosting model predicts both at once, blending three views of a molecule: learned structural patterns, computed descriptors, and measured lab properties. It beat single-task versions on both targets across repeated tests, with one weak spot for very low distribution volumes. Predicting the pair together could save costly lab work when screening candidate medicines.
plos-pone-0348273:
Xiao and Zhao, in a 2026 language study, compare degree adverbs, words like very, rather, and slightly, in news writing from mainland China and Taiwan. The two Mandarin varieties share most grammar, yet these small intensifiers are where they drift apart most. The team built news corpora from both sides and profiled how each adverb behaves.

Both sides favored strong and middling intensifiers and avoided the most extreme and weakest ones, though Taiwan used extreme forms more. What the adverbs modified differed: mainland writers more often boosted verbs and whole predicates, while Taiwan writers more often boosted adjectives and descriptive phrases. The words being boosted also carried a more positive tone on the mainland. Grouping the adverbs showed each side's special forms have close substitutes on the other side. The authors offer the profiles as a resource for dictionaries and for teaching the two varieties apart.
plos-pone-0348373:
María García de Santos and colleagues reviewed fourteen years of cases of spinal epidural abscess, a dangerous pocket of infection beside the spinal cord, at a single hospital. Doctors often try antibiotics alone before surgery, but when that gamble fails, patients can be left paralysed. Among seventy-six patients in the 2026 study, most started on medicines only.

That approach failed in more than four of ten cases, and a quarter of those patients needed rescue surgery anyway.
